div.head: SUCCESSFUL SALE OF WORK.
div.p: A SUCCESSFUL SALE OF WORK.

St. Paul's Church and its Institutions. In accordance with along-standing custom, the annual sale of work in connection with St. Paul's Church fer parochial purposes was held in Kendrick-street school- room on Monday. This room was recently damaged by fire, but it has since been entirely renovated and fitted with moveable glass screens. On Monday it looked at its beet when it was the scene of the annual sale of work. There were a,•number of attractive stalls all arranged to the best advantage in chnege of a large number of willing workers. The following is a list of those in -charge of the stalls No. I stall (Workingparty), Mrs. Gibson Smith, Mrs. Chorley, Mrs. Lord and Miss Dora Reid. No. 2 stall, Mrs. Ilepherd and the Misses Geddes. No. 3 stall, Mrs. Burgess, M. Bunch and Mrs. Truslove. No. 4 stall, the Misses Finney and Miss Fowler. No. 5 stall (dolls), 'Miss Bracecautp and the Misses Jolley. No. 6 stall (the Vicarage), Mrs. Bracecamp, Mrs. Lindley, Mrs. J. Lawton nni Mrs. Locker. N 0.7 stall, Mrs. Curtis, Miss Bainbridge, Miss Seward and Miss Ethel Pierpoint. Flowerstall, the Misses Wainwright and 'Greenough. Working Men's stall, Mrs. Parsonage and Mrs. Turner Cooper. - , Refreshment Stoll, Mrs. Beesley, Mrs. Paul and the Misses Westwell, Braide, Smethurst (2), Picktyon, Houghton, Rogers and Ashurst. Bran Tub, Misses Kathleen Ifrenkireson, Dolly Par- sonage and Ada Collins. An effort was made to make the sale,auccess which was - the first since the Vicar(Rev. W.Bracecamp)wasrespons- ible for the work of the parish. In this respect the promoters were successful as they succeeded in their ambition to raise £3OO. The amount •actually taken -was £297 but this sum was increased to £3OO by several friends. The opening ceremony was performed by Mrs. Vero Davies. She was accompanied on the •platform by the Vicar and the churchwardens (Messrs. R. J. Charley . and J. H. Smethurst). The Viean, who was cordially recalved, explained the object of the gathering,and said all ehurch people realized hew difficult it was in these days to carry on it church work in the centre of a town. it was found that they were 'continually losing friends. They had lost a -xery good friend in the person of Mrs.Beamont; and the -result was that they were obliged to hold sales like the present to enable them to carry on their parochial organizations. They were asked to provide £3OO to help the assistant clergy fund. They only gat a grant of t 55 from the Additional Curates' Society, and the rest of the money required had to be raised by subscriptions . and the sale of work. He hoped all present would do their best to assist them, as the congregation at St. • Paul's helped themselves as well as they could,as would, have been seen from the reports of the vestry meeting, which had recently appeared in ,the newspapers. They hadraised in the church during the past 12 months no • less a sum than £5lO, mid he thought that fact spoke volumes fer the neople. (Applause). In that sum they • did not reckof the pew rents or the collection made every Sunday afternoon at the Men's Bible Class but what was collected Sunday morning and evening at the Church. It would be thus seen that they tried to help themselves, and that being the case theyhad every confidence in appealing to their friends outside the parish on an occasion like- the present for aid. It was a great pleasure to them to have Mrs. Davies with them because he understood this would be the first time she • had ever opened a sale of work. The Davies family had . alvzsays'been interested in St. Paul's. Mr. Robert Davies did a great deal for them, and he was also thankful to be able to say that Mr. Vere Davies had also helped -them considerably. He hoped that this would be the :most successful sale they had everhad. In conclusion the Vicar,said he hadto apologise for the absence of the :late Vicar, Mr. Tarbuck, but he had sent his better half ,and they were all very pleased to see Mrs. Tarbuck. (Applause.) He must also apologise for the absence of :the Rev. S. Wilkinson (a former vicar of St. Paul's) and Mrs. Wilkinson. He was, however, thankful to see :another vicar, of St. Paul's, the Rev.H. V. Pigot, with them, and the other clergy. (Applause.) He hoped this would be the most- successful sale they had ever had as -this was the first function of the kind at St. Paul's for -which he was responsible. (Applause.) Mrs. VERE B. DA-VIES, in performing the opening yceremony, said she had very much pleasure in declaring the sale opetesand she hoped that as this was Mr. Brace- camp's first year, the ,proceeds would be particularly, successful. (Applause.) Alderman Surros proposed a vote of ;thanks to Mrs. I Davies and said he took a deep interest,in the church because he had attended it nearly all his life. It was eratifving to have a lady to open the sate who was the Zlaugh-ter-in-law of one"of the oldest and bqst friends of the church. Mr. Robert Davies had takenaeleep interest in the church as long as he could remember, and had

Mr. J. H. SMETHURST, in seconding, said they had heard much about Mr. Davies and his family, and they agreed with every word, but they must not forget that Mrs. Vere Davies was also the representative of an old Warrington family, and was delighted to back up her husband in the good work he did for the parish of St. Paul's and ,other parishes. (Hear, hear.) The motion was heartily agreed to. . _ .

Mr. VERE DAVIES, in res-ponding on behalf of his wife, said her father and his family had been connected with St. Paul's for many years, and he could remember as a small boy going to the church in, he believed, the time of the Rev. Dr. Massingham. He was now associ- ated with St. Paul's by being one of the trustees of the living and he thought he might claim that he had some share in offering the living to Mr. Bracecamp, and that was one of the best things the trustees ever did for the parish. Mr. Bracecamp was certainly thetright man in the right place—(applause)—and all he could say in con- elusion was that as this was the age of record breaking he hoped the present sale of work would qstablish record for the Vicar. (Applause.) I - The sale was then entered upon and continued until a late hour in the evening.

div.head: WHAT CONSTIPATION CAUSED. A Young Lady's Escape From Death.
div.p: WHAT CONSTIPATION CAUSED. A Young Lady's Escape From Death.

Constipation if neglected, often leads to stoppage of the bowels. Chas. Forde's Bile Beans cure constipation by stimulating the liver to natural action, and in this way they saved Miss Ettie Palmer, of Back 253, Great Colmore-street, Birmingham, from a serious operation. in the Queen's Hospital, and probably from death. Miss Palmer says In my case, constipation and digestive disorders led,to a stoppage of the bowels. I could not take nourishment, and consequently grew too feeble to work. Having taking to my bed, I got weaker tand weaker. It was not thought I should live. Indeed, the clergyman of the parish came to pray at my bedside, so near death was I. The doctor called in a physician, and it was said my only hope of life lay in an operation which might or might not be successful. I was taken to the Queen's Hospital, and prepared for operation, but at the last moment my parents stopped all the proceedings and hadrae taken back home. This was in consequence of what they had ,heard about the power of Bile Beans, and I was started upona course immediately. From the first,l improved .and in a few days my bowels were acting normally. I ;gradually got stronger, and in a short time I was back at work. Since then I have worked for twelve months,and have never had a trace of my old complaint. That ,speaks eloquently for the permanence of Bile Bean cures. 1 ;was so weak at the time I was taken to hospital for the operation,thatl believe 1 should never have lived - through it." 'The above sensational facts coming to the ears of a representative of a popular newspaper, he at once in- vestigated them. He found that, interesting as were the details g iven,there was no doubt as to their accuracy. Indeed he discovered that the whole details had been embodied in a declaration and sworn to before Mr. J. Seymour Price, a Birmingham Commissioner for Oaths. There can be no doubt that this incident forms one of the most striking proofs ,obtainable of the'. value of this great vegetable specific. Bile Beans cure constipa- tion, giver ailments, headache, indigestion, female ail- ments and irregularities, pimples and skin eruptions. Obtainable from all medicine vendors at is. 11d. or 2s. 9d. per box. Avoid substitutes.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE AT WARRINGTON.
Brushworks Gutted in Bridge-street.

A disastrous tire occurred at Warrington on Tuesday morning. At five o'clock Police Constable Bennet was on defy in Bridge-street when he detected the smellof burning. On making an investigation he found that the brush works of Mr. H. Jackson at the rear of the Royal Oak Inn, were ablaze. .He promptly aroused the in- mates of the public house and information of the out- break was sent to the Fire Engine Station. In the meantime the .constable with the assistance of Sergeant Bell removed :a number of hOrSes from the stables of Mr. William Russell, cab proprietor, adjoining the works. A full complement of firemen quickly turned. out under -the direction of Superintendent Turner and Deputy-Superintendent Turner, 'with the steam fire engine "Captain," and various appliances. On arriving in Bridge-street itwas found that the fireiand obtained a very firm hold, and the brigade directed their efforts to confining it to the brush works. In this they were successful, the stables being saved. The Atraw, hay, and fodder in the stables were removed by employes. The works • were com- pletely gutted and the stock. of brushes was destroyed. The flames burnt through the centre beam, and conse- quently tha roof fell W. Some rooms on the ground floor in the occupation of Mr. McClinton were con- siderably damaged and a stock of cigars was lost. There were several barrels of spirits in one of the rooms but these were saved. The total damage to the buildings, stock, &c., is roughly estimated at £l,OOO and is partly covered by insurance.

Indepensient Order of Rechabites Warrington Juvenile District No,. 4. The qu'Arterly meeting of the (Usti-ict was held in Brick-street Miss ion schoolroom, Wa rrington .on Satur- I day. The Council was called to .order at 3.30 p,m. by Bro. H. Blacker of Bryan supported by I the whole of the District officers and representatives ! from the 14 juvenile branches forming the District as well as several visitors from the adult tests being I present. Bro. Massey, D.S. submitted the report of 1 the executive for the past quarter which showed that the work of the District Continued to increase both ,numerically and financially, there being an increase cf 5:2 meinbers during the past quarter be.sides j transferring four :juveniles to the advlt tents. .I The best increase from one tent was from Jonadab tent Warrington, whose meeting place- was hi the mision room,also several other tents _showed good work had been dOne by 'increasing their numbers, making the total membership of the -district 641, and ' after paying all dues and one funeral claim :on the death of a member there was a balance on the quarter of £l7 17s. Old. making the total funds of the dis- trict £.230 7s. 6-Id. Bro. Wright, D.S.J.T. presented his report which was of a most encpuraging character I the tents having done exceedingly well,but the future prospects were even more hopeful and promised evemi'. more gratifying results in the fdture than in the past quarter. There were at least three new juvenile branches that the executive were expect- ing would in all probability- .be opened in the course of the next quarter. It was decided to accept the invitation of Triumphant tent to hold the next district meeting at Ashton. After the business,a splendid knife and fork tea was pro- vided by the superintendent of Jonadab tent. Bro. Blacker moved a vote of thanks to the friends at Brick-street for their hospitality, this being seconded by Bro. Walter Hulme. Bro. B. Warburton responded on behalf of the tent. -

A Parliamentary correspondent of the "Daily News" states that a proposal is on foot for founding a new club, consisting of young Nonconformist members of Parliament and leading workers and advocates in the Nonconformist cause. The suggestion is to follow in the main,the lines of work adopted by the Eighty Club.

" 1 what, use did he malze of his good !cooks': ii“ deceived everyone." " He did not." "He did. You know he did, Ar.ll-, I believe myself .he was at one time after the -daughter of old Jinnev, and would have married her." Mrs. Tremewan rose with the wrath of Pn offertded woman. "Mart,' that--that creature !" she cried, shrilly. "The daughter of a smuggler—

lf an ugly " Sha was good-looking then," interrupted Ilannaford, "and her father's character was quite as good as old Pillage's. He was suspected of smuggling himself, and of running cargoes some- where abort the neighbourhood of Bolt Head. However, that is an old story. We have both grown a trifle warm, Mrs. Tremewan; The widow interrupted with a glance. T "You said ' Amy ' a short time ago 1" "We have both grown a trifle warm," repeated Mr. Hannaford, re-seating himself. "Let us conduct this conversation on more reasonable lines if you please. As to Walter Pil- •lage, -I say, again, he was a scamp. I can now un- derstand how he got that money from the old man. It was Ellen Jinney who persuaded her fathcr to lend it. A.h, poor girl, if she had only known the use it was to be put to !" "I don't see why you should object to the use," said Mrs. Tremewan. "Miss Ellen Jinney would have objected. She was in love with Pillage, and mourned his end for many a long clay. I expect that it is for his sake she is single now. With that publichonse and her money she could have. married over and over again amongst her own people, but "Then she should keep to her own people," said Mrs. Tremewan crossly. "But let us say no more about her, George. I wish you to undemtand that When I was in London I married Walter." "You were engaged to me at the time," remarked Hanna.ford. sternly. The widow had the grace to blush. "Yes, I was," she admitted candidly. "Oh, don't look at me like that George, I know I acted badly, but I am being punished for it, terribly punished." She waited for some itim. of sympathy, but as none came she resumed. `l. intended to teal you when I returned from Hampsteaa. Indeed I did." "Lb was, too late then, if your story is to be believed," replied her old lover in an icy tone; "you were married. May I ask Why you parted with your husband after deceiving both me and your parents?" "It was on account of Walter's poverty," anewered Mrs. Treinewan, letting her head drOop ; "he was poor, and could net keep me. He had an offer from a friend to go to India and work on a tea-plantation. It was agreed between us that he should go, and that when he was settled I was to join him. He went shortly after I returned to my parents, and they knew nothing about the marriage. My friend at Haanpstead kept our secret. ' "And you kept your secret from me, also!" he said-, bitterly. "I could not help myself. Walter made me promise to tell no one until he gave me leave. But at least, George," added Mrs. Tremewan, with dignity, "at least I did what I could. I broke off our engagement." "You did, 'and broke my heart at the same time. No," he waved his hand impatiently, "don't say anything. My heart is all right now, and it is ridiculous for two old people like us to talk senti- ment." "Old people?" cried Mrs. Tremewan, indig- nantly, and bit her lip. "I beg your pardon," said Hannaford, with an ironical bow. "I know that women never 'grow old. What 'I mean to say is that I want you to keep to the point of your story. You married. Pil- lage, and broke off with me. • "Yes," said the widow, somewhat annoyed at this cold-blooded dissection of her old romance. "I thought it only right. But as I had promised 'Walter I could not tell my real reason for break- ing the engagement. I forget what reason I did give."
"So do I," replied Hannaford, cheerfully. "No znattecr. Go on.
." How cruel you are, George!" sighed tot widow. " Ttgen you went abroad." . .
" Yes ! I remained abroad for two years. When I returned to Dartbridge you were married and living at The Gray lIouse.":, • ." That is true. The news came when I was in

Landon that Walter was lost at sea. There was no doubt about it. I went to see the underwriters myself, and they told me that every soul on board the ship had perished. I mourned Walter in secret, as I did not, dare then to .00nfess the truth. Then Tremewan came and proposed to' me. You were absent, and my mother insisted that I should marry Tee wan. There was no help for it. I did. He has been a good, kind husband to me," she went on, "but I would never have married him had Iliad my way. But my another ! She was too clever for me."
`.` Not clever enough to prevent your marriagr with Pillage," said Mr. Hannaford.
"Did she ever know?" "No. She never knew." "Your husband. 4)Did he know?"

"He .did not. He was so jealous that I believe he would have left me had he known the truth. He was ignorant all the days of his life. I am glad of t. He was always good to me, and I sihould have been sorry to. see him unhappy." She ()eased to speak, and Hannaford looked silently at her. Then a thought occurred which =de him flu Sh. "Dora," said he. "What of Dora?"

Mrs. Tremewan guessed his meaning; and flushed in turn. "Dora is the daughter of Francis 'fre- mewan," he replied; "it was .three years after I parted from Walter-that she was born. If you are drinking that ohe has any of Walter's blood in her veins you are trnistaken. You can certainly let !her marry your son with--ah, .poor Will! How is the?"

"I don't know why you dhould trouble to ask," said the old man trembling. "Be is in gaol m. the charge of murdering yourhusiband, as you know." "If I thought he was guilty, I certainly should not have come to see you, George. But I am sure that he is innocent, and that his innocence will be proved. Oh yes; he will go free to marry Dora."
"Do you now anything likely to prorc:e his in- nocence?" •

"No. lam quite ignorant ivho killed Francis. He had many enemies, as he was always a violent- tempered man. But I know of no one who would have murdered him. My 'belief that Will—well, you see it's premonition,' she said, and broke off with a shrug. "I don't put anucili faith in premonitions," responded Mr. Hannaford, in a gloomy tone. "How- ever, if you did not come to see me about my un- happy boy, why did you come at all? To discuss our foolish love story?"

Mrs. Tremewan Shook her head, and her face began to ()Tow white again as sthe remembered her great (trouble." I came to ask for your aid." "Anything I .can do," began Hannaford, when she cut him short.
"Ah, that is the questiori. Can you do any- thing? Find Walter. Find Walter. That is all I,ask."

Hanna,f ord stared. "Pillage? He is dead," he said, in A wondering tone. "So I thought," she continued, clasping her hands. "God 'help me! I thought he was dead and at the bottom of the sea, and long long have I mourned +him. But the other day Paul Vane--"
"Your late husband's nephew?" "Yes. He came to s,ay that he had seen Walter alive three years ago." "Impossible. He could kncyw nothing of Pil- lage,"

-••• So I 'aid—so I said,'! cried Mrs. Tremewan. "But he pinked Walter up on the street one winter night,—but listen, George. I will tell you au that Paul said;" and Mrs. Trethewa.n rapidly de- tailed Vane's story.

Mr. Hannaford listened in silence} only he won- dered at the punishment that was being dealt out to this woman. The*girlish follies of her youth were indeed bearing fruit. Even before she had ended he saw her position. "Then you were never really the wife of Tre- inewan?" he cried pacing the room, his •face filled with amazement. 4" No—that is if Walter is still alive. I swear, George, I. thought he was dead., I made nil en- quiries at the time. before I married Tremesfa,n. if I had thought for one moment that he was alive I should 'not have married FrtneiS. I loved Walter best. But. if he is alive why has .he kept, away from me all this .time? He. knew I loved him—him only !"

"I suppose he' has been 'reading Enoch Arden,". said Hannaford, a trifle cynically. "Perhaps he thought you were happy with Trtmewan." "happy !" echoed the widow, with scorn.- " yes. .1 was happy in a way. But any 'heart brake- when Walter died. Can he be alive,—oh, how can 1 learn!"
'She was thoroughly in earnest, and looked at Hannaford with clasped haaids in an imunitsriac

CHAPTER XV

div.head: OLD LOVE.'
div.p: THE OLD LOVE.'

If there was 0410 thing which Mr. Hannaford disliked it was being taken by surprise. Yet this unpleasant thing happened on the very night he returned ,from London. He had arrived by the seven-thirty train, and after making a poor dinner, was seated in his study gazing into the fire. He was a good deal worried, for his consul- tation with the solioitor had ,resulted in nothing tangible. Under the circumstances, and in spite of the enormity of the accusation, there was just a chance of getting- Will out of prison on bail. But as regards 'his chances of leaving the court without a ,stain on his character—as the saying goes—the eminent solicitor had thought very little of them. He heard. all that Hannaford had to sal, and shook this head. When he did speak it was to the effect that Will was the last pert wthb had seen Trermewan alive, and it depended .upon himself to prove that he'had left him alive. This was but cold comfort to Hannaford, . and be now sat over his fire in the lowest of spirits. There was no chance of saving Will, so far as he *mad see. Yet he was certain that the boy was guiltless. But how to prove his innocence? While the old genttleman worried 'over this question, and worried in vain, the door opened • slowly, and he turned his head expecting to see his servant. He was just about to rebuke her for disturbing him at this hour When he saw that the new coiner was a stranger. At least, so he thought,. at the first glance, and he rose in some surprise at what he considered an unwarrantable intrusien. _But_ when she glided forward and _

threw herself at his feet, he recognised, with dis- may and astonishment, that A was Mrs. Tremewan who had thus thrust herself an his privacy. . "I am in trouble—great (trouble !" she cried, ca.-tea:Ling his hand, and looking up with the tears streamiing down her face, "and I came to pan— to my dear old friend, for aid. I knew you would not admit me, .so I slipped past the servant, and came in without an invitation. Oh, George, pity me 1" •

While she was sobbing at his feet and holding his hand, the servant a2pmred at the door looking at once puzzled and indignant, Mr. Hannaford did not care to be thus found with a weeping woman who called him by his Christian name, so he hastily withdrew his hand, and went to the door. The maid retreated before the pallor of hiS face:

"It is Mrs. Tremewan," whispered her master, quickly; ".he has not yet recovered from the death of her husband. Leave me with her for a time. •I will ring when I want you. Say no word of this to the other servants. If you do I shall dismiss you instantly."

" Yes, sir," replied Ole maid, and ,when she found the door shut in her face went up to her own bedroom. She felt that if she appeared in the servants' hall -just at present she would not be able to hold her tongue. And as heir present place was a good one she did not wish to run the risk af losing it. Thus it came about that no one, save the maid, aforesaid, knew that Mrs. Tete- mewan had wept at the feet. of Mr. Hannaford, and had called him "George." He went back to her. ,She was still on her knees,—and taking her by the hand drew her to her feet. "Sit down and compose yourself, Mrs. Tremewan," he said as quietly as he could; "there is no need to make s scene. Whatever your trouble is I will help you for the sake of old times."

Mrs. Tremewan moaned and wiped her eyes. She was really in great trouble, and looked much older than her years. All her dainty, fragile beauty was gone, and Hantraford was amazed when he beheld her tear-stained 'face, and saw how carelessly she was dressed. Mrs. Tremaewan had always been so particular about what she wocre. There must be something very, wrong, he thought, to put her in such a state. "What is it ?" he asked, seating ,himself, and glancing at her ire a cold and critical manner.

She caught no note of kindness in his voice. He spoke as coolly as a judge might do. And this was their first conversation since she had jilted him more than twenty years before Yet she had thought that the sight .of her would have awakened the old tenderness. . Perhaps if She had been her usual composed, carefully-dressed self, Mr. Hannaford -faight have been moved, for she was a remarkably well-preserved woman for her age. But in this disordered attire, with p, pale flea and swollen red-rimmed eyes, she was not an object of romance. If she had hoped to in- flueneo George Hannaford by recalling the past she had failed in her attempt. However, she could not believe that she had so failed, for her vanity was great. She essayed an imploring tone, with a free use of her eyes. -
"George," she said, gazing at him beseechingly. " Oh, GecTge!" _ _ _ _ _
"1 think -we had better not make use af that name," replied Mr. Hannaford, in icy tones. "1
should .not- think of calling you 'Am.'" "It was 'Amy' and ' Geomge ' between us once."

"Many, anany years ago-, Mrs. Tremelvan,— when we were both young and both foolish,—l, at least, for I believed that you loved me." "1 did--4—No," she broke off, as she saw the steely gleam in his eyes, "it is no use saying that I did. .1 never loved you. It was my parents who. wanted meto marry you."

" •And-yo-u preferred :rremewan," said Hamra- ford, shading his face with his hand. He did not wish to look more than he could help at that ruined beauty which he had so madly loved. "1 did not prefer Tremewan," cried his widow, pa,stionatelly. loved Waster Pillage. Yes! You may well be astonished, George. I loved Walter. ;--never anyone but him." In that case why did you not marry him?" Mrs. Tremewan braced herself to make a confes- sion. "I did," the said, in a low tone of voice, and stared at the carpet. She did not dare to look into the eyes of the main she had wronged. Hannaford stafted to his feet.
"Why do you say •that?" he cried, in an agi- tated tone. "How cam you have married Pillage when for the last twenty-five years you have been the wife of Tremewan?"

Mrs. Tremewan, her eyes still on be ground, explained. "When I was in London—during my first season . "And your last," said George Hannaford, harshly. "I remember. I come to London,—so did Francis. We thought that some of the dandies might carry you off, and we both loved you madly. But never knew that he was there at the time."
"He 'followed me up just as you and Francis did."

Mr. Harmaford•shook his head. "That is im- possible," he replied; "Pillage was too poor to get away from these pants. He and, his mother lived in the old tall, on the moor, like two mice in a church. They had barely sufficient to keep themselves a:ive."

"Oh ! I know he was poor," said Mrs. 'lre- mewan, • bitterly; if he had not been I ehould have married him with the consent of nar parents. 'As it .was I married him secretly." "Secretly? Whore did you marry him?" "In Landon," and Mrs. Tremewan gave the name of the church. "He and I were so fond of one another," she continued. "He was mad for me to be his wife, and I loved him so. I was sup- posed to be on a visit to a friend at Hampstead. She was romantic, and helped us. We were Married, as I say, and we lived together at Hamp- stead. Walter had enough money to pay for a cottage."
"Where did he got the money?" asked Hanna- ford, sitting down, and looking paler than ever, for the news touched him nearly. You

"It was Old Jirmey who lent' it to him. remember old Jinney, George?" " Yes ! lie kept The Eight Bells public- house,—his daughter keeps it now. Old Jinnev had money, I know, but I should mot have thought he was the man to lend it to a wastrel and a scamp as ho must have known Pillage to be. I have offended you," he said, as Mrs. Tremewan looked up angrily. "Yes, you have," she said, defiantly." Why should you pall Walter these aaames? He was of an old family, even if he was poor. And how handsome--" .
" Haadsoane enotteh." said Mr. Nazknallard.,

attitude. It .wouid. 11441 re 24.17 .I.crgeri the dead man—the man alleged to be aliie—but when Hannaford remembered her life for the post twenty years, and her love for dramatic effect, he wandered if she really wanted Piltage to turn up again. "Remember you will lose Tremewan's for- tune," he said, looking at her keenly. "I know that Paul claims it. But can he— can he—" she demanded.
"I think so. If the will left the property to you ass Tremewan's wife, it oan he set aside, if it can be proved that you are no wife." . _ _ _ _ _ _

"And Dora?" taitered Mrs. Tromewan. " Ah, poor Dora 1" said Hannaford, "her position is indeed painful. She has no name—no position—no money. But Oat, does not matter. Will can give her all three, and love into the bar- gain." "Lit Will is in gaol." "I know it. Why !remind me of so obvious a fact! You were always so fond of detail. My son will be set free, and will marry Dora. I have read° up my mind to that. This Paul Vane. as he been here before?"
"Nit for some years. He quarrelled with Francis."
"Dc*s he say that?" demanded Hannalord, quickly. "Say what?" she asked curiously. "That this is his first visit of recent years." "Yes. He never

Mr. H,artnaford interrupted her by snapping fingers exultingly. "That is din right, Mrs. Tre- mewan. Say no more. I will see Vane to- morrow. Where is he?" "At the Nelson Hotel." " Ah ! I thought he would have gone somewhere else."

"Why should he? Do you know anything?" "Leave it to me, Mrs. Tremewan," said Hanna ford, and he looked bright and confident. "I Imo* what I know. You return home and do not trouble your head about this probable loss of for- tune."
"Do you think I sivairlose it? Con say pro- bable."

" I used the word wrongly. I should say this possible loss of fortune. I wilil ask Vane to produce Pillage alive. The man must be recognised by you before Vane's claim to your husband's fortune oan be admitted." "You are sure—sure?"

" Quite sure. In ray eyes. and in the eYes of the world you will be Mrs. Tremowain, and Dora Miss Tremewan until Pillage ireappears. Vane says he is alive. Vane must produce him. Go home and sleep well, Mrs. Tramowan. I wilcoall on Vane to morrow."

Mrs. Tremewau would have spoken, but the effort after what she thad undergone was too much for her. She burst into tears, and left the room. Mr. Hannaford did not see her out. "I shall save my boy after all," he said.

div.head: CLAIMANT,
div.p: THE CLAIMANT,

The Nelson Hotel, in High Street, was one al those old-fashioned inns which aim e rapidly disap- pearing before the glare and glitter of the more modern caravanseries. llts rooms were small and gloomy, and crowded with ancient ,furniture of the Georgian Era. The Nelson might have been up- to-date about the time -when its namesake was winning the Battle of the Nile, but now it was iar behind the times. Yet it still continued to be the principal hotel in Damtbridg,e, and in spite of its antiquity was extzemedy comfortable. The food if plain was well-cooked and well served; the head-waiter looked like an larchbishop, and the port wine he dispensed was undeniable port which .cannot, always fbe said of the modern vin- tage. The archbishop-waiter gave it only to favoured custoinens, and ,ainongst these was, Paul Vane.

Vane was indeed a favourite with the domestics of the Nelson Hotel. He was generous, he gave small trouble, ancl was always polite 'when any- thing was done for him. Therefore the servants approved of him, and were willing to do what they could. The landlord, a burly man who usually sat and gossiped in the bar, approved of his guest, and frequently regaled Ldm with the scandal of the aleighbourhood, of which he had a great store. As he knew that this young man was the nephew of the deceased, Mr. Tremewan, he did, not touch upon the topic of the murder. And Vine never asked him to do so. As yet the claim against Mins. Tremewan was not known. The time was not ripe to proclaim her marrlage with the dead man illegal, and for reasons beet known to himself, it appeared that Vane was obliged to act cautiously. He was fond of pampering himself, and had this roorms on the first floor, •the best accommodation that the hotel could afford. His income was not large enough to guarantee this outlay, but he was so certain of obtaining possession of the Tre- wan estates (that he did not stint himself. Re occupied the best apartments, he ordered the best food and wines, and in .anticipatiori of his good fortune got for himself aLl•tthat his heart could desire. And this was no small thing, for Paul's desires were limited only by the amount of money at his disposal. .Had he been a millionaire he coruld easily have spent the money solely on him- :self. His selfishness was an abyss which would have swallowed up the fortunes of Aladdin. _

It was one afternoon at three o'clocii that Mr. Hannaford called to see this sybarite. Paul had just finished a dainty little Ituicheon, and was now smoking a prime cigar, with a cup of coffee at his elbow. The weather being yet cold, a good Are was burning, and Paul's comfortable armchair. was drawn up (to the blaze. - He was contented and rather drowsy, so he did not welcome the appearance of Mr. Hannalord's card .with any en- thusiasm. As a matter of fact he ,swore. All the same, he gave orders that the visitor was to be Shown up. For obvious reasons Vane wished to Make ,friends with all the Darthridge people, of whom Mr. Hanna-ord was one of the most influen- tial. Moreover—as .Paul knew from oommon gossip—he had no very great love for Mrs. 'Pre- mewan ; so he determined to make use of this enmity to forward his own ,schemes. It had been in his mind to call upon Mr. Hannaford, end he was very much astonished when th 4 gentlemiEun called to see him. But he wa,s ;too. diplomatic to show any surprise in his .greeting, and 'welcomed his visitor quite as a matter of course. ~. • "I am glad to see you, sir,". he said, advancing towards his guest with mitstretched hand; "this is an unexpected pleasure." Perhaps -it was because Hannaford was looking for a chair that he did not see Mr. Vane's hand, but he certainly did not take it, and Paul, with rather an uncomfortable feeling, was obliged to withdraw it. "He comes as an enemy," he :thought, while still smiling. "I wonder if he knows about my claim? If he does, he ought to be glad," and he took. a seat. "Will you have a cigar, Mr. Itannaford?" he said, not at all rebuffed by the brusque manner of the old gentleman. "No? A glass of *wine, them? No Coffee? There is good coffee here." "I will take nothing thank you, Mr. Vane," replied Hannaford; stiffly; "my errand here is to see you on rather unpleasant business."

• "Indeed. I am unaware that I have offended you," said Paul blandly. "Oh, it has nothing to do with me," replied Mr. Hannaford, twirling his ivhite moustache. "I ought to apologise for fiqving called to see you without an introduction. But when I explain my errand I am sure you will pardon my apparent freedom."

Vanowaved his de:icate hand languidly. "You are pardoned already; sir," he said. "Anything I can do "—the waved his 'hand again and looked unutterable things. Ali the s6,me, and in spite .of his assumed languor, .he was very much on the (alert., The opening of the conversation, was ominous.

"Very good," said Mr. Ha.nnafard, leaning his .hands on his stick, and looking at Paul from under his bushy eye-brows, "let me get to ,bus,iness. To put the matter in a nuitshel, Mr. Vane, my old friend, Mrs. Tremewan, has informed me Of your claim to the Trernewan estates."

Paul was rather prepared for this announcement, therefore he was not so much astonished as his visitor expected him to be. "Your old friend, Mrs. Tremewan?" he repec.ted, with a faint 'sneer. " Common report - " "Is a:common liar sr," cried the fir y old gentle- man. "I did not 'come here to gossip, but to in- quire about your claim." "And you are here on behalf of Mrs. Tre- mem-an ?"

". I am," said Mr. Hannaford, shortly. Paul shrugged his elegant shoulders, and smiled at his stern visitor. "I can put the matter in a nutshell also, Mr. Hannaford; said he coolly. "I have reason to believe that the lady who calls her self Mrs. Tremewan has no right to the na.ane. That is all." • _ _
"And quite enough, too," grunted Mr. Hamm" food ; "-Your 2-3,ounls for soxina so ?"

'She was married to a man calied Vv alter Pil- lage, in London, before she married my uncle," replied Vane, promptly.. "Here is a copy of the certificate of marriage." He threw it across to his 'visitor, having taken it from his breast pocket. The Old man looked at it, Ad it appeared to be in order. But he did not need this assurance that the marriage had taken place. He already knew as much from Mrs. Tremewan. "That is all right," he replied, giving back the certificate, "but Mrs. Tremewan 'married her second husband after the death of the first. The late Walter Pillage was drowned at sea—in the Indian Ocean, if you want to be precise." • "It is. always as well to be precise in matters of this sort," said Vane, replacing the certificate in his pocket-book, "but you are wrong, Mr. Han- naford. Walter Pillage was not drowned. He escaped with some others in a small boat. He way detained on the Asian coast for some years in a kind of honourable captivity, and ultimately managed to get away to England." "Indeed!' Who told you this?" "Pillage himself," repied Vane, promptly, and proceeded to narrate 'the story he had already told Mrs. Tremewan and her daughter. Mr. .Hanna- ford had heard it from the widow, but he was quite content to, hear it again, so as to see if the two accounts tallied. They did. ", So Pillage, aecording to you, was alive three years ago?" he said. " Very gaud. Where is he now? You know,. of course. I hardly think you would have advanced this claim airless you were able to pro- duce him." Vane rose and began to pace the room. Across his delicate face the colour swept in rapid waves. Several times he +attempted to speak, but somehow the words stuck in his throat., .Mr. Ha.nnaford quite enjoying this embarrassment, although he could not divine the reason, kept his eye fixed steadily on the young man. "Gain you produce Pillage?" he demanded pitilessly. "I am not sure," said Vane, compelled at length to speak; "the man has disappeared again, and I do not know where to look for him." " Ah, I thought so 1" sneered Hannaford. "Then, of course, you are aware - that until the man is found--if, indeed, he is alive—Mrs. Tre- 'mew= must be looked upon as the widow of your uncle, and will remain in possession Of the pro- party." - "I know that. But I intend to advertise far Pillage." "Be sure you advertise for the right one, Mr. Vane. I know Pillage well. I was a friend and rival of his when I was young.. If an impostor
corays forward, I can unmask- him.'

Vane turned hotly on his- guest. " Perlraps yot intend to accuse me of getting someone to pla3 the part?" he said angrily. "If you do, it will not be of much use," re torted Ifr.l42,lThafoirci. "I know Pillage, and ii the true man comes fdivard I shall be the firsi to acknowledge him. But I may tell you, Mr. Vane, that I don't believe in this story. You are a poor man—that is you have only a small income. quite inadequate to the gratification of yam luxurious tastes. You wish to obtain your uncle': money, and this statement of yours is ma.de'wher the man is dead and cannot deny the truth of it." "ho told you all this about my privats affairs?" demanded Vane, furiously. "My son, Will. You know him Mr. Vane. You made a, friend of him. He learned much about you, which he told me." "Ah 1" sneered Vane, who had turned a trifle pale. "I thought I was confiding in a man pf honour; but it seems

• "Silence, six 1" Cried Mr. Hannaford, rising ,and striking his (stick on die floor. "You Shall not speak against ,my son. He is in prison under suspicion of murder. You know if he is innocent or not."
"I !" Vane was now livid and recoiled. "Dc you then accuse anie NA the murder of my uncle, Mr. Hannaford?"

"Who had so much to gain by the death'?" re- torted the ,old gentleman. "I do not say that you strangled the man yourself. I should not think you lhad the counage to do it. But Ido say that you know something about the crime."
"I do not,'." pansi;e' d Vane; "how dare you say so?"

"I say so because I know you were in this town on the night the crime was committed. You stayed. here—at this very hotel. You arrived in the morning, and you went away the next morning. You never went near your uncle during the day— 'but at night "I was not there either," cried Vane, sharply;, "I was in Dartbiidge on the fifteenth of January. I was here—in this hotel as you say. I gave my own name—l did not pretend to be other than my- self. Does that look as if I were guilty? I came down to ask my uncle to help me, as I was so deeply in debt. If it came to the worst I in- tended to break my promise to Pillage and to tell my uncle tiaat he was aiive. But I could not summon up courage to go to The Gray House until the morning after my arrival. You know what a bully my uncle was. I was afraid; I am not ashamed to confess it. Tremewau was a devil. I did not desire to see him in the evening. I waited till the maiming of the sixteenth. Then I heard that he had been found dead. I was un- willing to stay lest I should Ari,et into trouble, and, moreover, I saw that I could get nothing at the time. I returned to London by the mid-day train, and only came down again a few days ago to claim the estates. But I deny that I had anything to do with the murder. 1 did not kill My uncle."
"I never accused you of doing so," replied Han- naford, tartly. "But I say !that you know who did it." . "How do you make that out?"

"Very simply. My information as, to your movements -comes from Grant, the boots of this hotel, who was dismissed some weeks ago. He was here when you were, on the sixteenth of January. He came to me for 'employment after he was dismissed. In the interest of my son, I mad‘ all enquiries as to what strangers were in Dart- bridge on the night of the crime." "And why? Did you think some stranger com- mitted. the crime?"

"I did. Tremewan, as you justly remark, was a devil, and had many enemies. I fancied that one might have come to Dartbridge to kill him. I, therefore, made enquiries, and as Grant came to me for employment I asked -what he knew relative to strangers stopping at the Nelson. He then told me that you came on the fifteenth and re- turned to London on the sixteenth."

"Whereupon you at once thought that I had killed my tinc:e," sneered Vane, wiping, his face, .and trying to appear calm. "I thought it was strange that when your, uncle 'was dead you .should run 'away so quickly. but I did not think you had anything to do with the matter at the time. Now, however, after I have heard your story and Mrs. Tremewan's, I am be- ginning to change my mind." "You think that I planned the crime." , "For someone else to carry out," said Mr. Hannaiord,.promptly ; " that is my belief. Grant told me that on the -night of the fifteenth you did not return till twelve o'clock.. Ile let you in, and he said that your clothes were torn and your face was muddy and cut. The man is a fool, and never thought of connecting you with the crime. Even now, when he has answered my questions he does not think that you have anything to do with the matter. But / think you have, Mr. Paul Vane," said Mr. Hannaford, drawing up his tall form to its fullest height, "and I want to know why yos, were out co late, and why you returned muddy and torn and bleeding." "I was muddy because I had fallen. I was torn because I lost my way .and got amongst some thorn bushes
"Or gorse bushes such as are round The Gray House?"

"I was not near The Gray House on that night," said Vane, hotly, "-and I was not bleeding." "Grant said that your face was scratched." "Ah, yes; now I remember. I did scratch my face when I fell amongst the thorns. But I deny that I was at The Gray House, or that I saw my uncle."

"Where were you then?" demanded Mr. Ilanna- ford, coldly. "I decline to say." • "Take care, Mr. Vane. Your conduct, is highly .suspiaiousi I havelhe interests of my son to look .after. 11 I liked I could have you arrested on

suspicion." "You dare-" began Vane hotly, then -cooled down. "1 can prove an alibi." "What is your alibi?" " I decline to tell you." "Will you tell it to the police?" "The police will not dare to arrest me." "We'll see about that !" said Mr. Hannafard, grimily, and moved towards the door. "See here, Mr. Paul Vane. As yet I do npt see my way. When I do, you had better look out for trouble. But if you wooly Mrs. Tremewan over this preposterous claim of yours, I'll have you &rested on Grant's evidence." div.head: TWENTY MINUTES LATE.
div.p: TWENTY MINUTES LATE.

All the way from King's Cross we had been steadily losing time. The rails were wet and the train unusually heavy. At York we were twenty minutes late. There the railway people attached an additional engine and the train entered the Waverley Station, Edinburgh, that night on time. The principle is commonplace: when you cannot diminish an excessive load, increase the power. But what is an excessive load? Gently, now. Wait a bit.

On any correct scale one hundred pounds is one • hundred pounds but on the back of a porter it is one thing and on the back of a slender girl quite another. To the first it is nothing to notice, to the second, it is crushing. In other words, weight is a question of what supports it. This, then, is the principle on which we are to under- stand Mrs. Margaret Williams' assertion that she was heavy some years ago. No doubt the weighing machine would have showed her some pounds off her proper. weight ; for she was ill, out of sorts, and not eating anything twspealr of. All the same, the lighter she got the heavier she felt; and when it comes to one's relation to one's Ovi,-n weight it is feeling, and not the scales,that settles the point. For several years she dragged along in this unsatis- factory way; always weary and fatigued, as if from hard and continuous labour, when, in fact, she was doinn, scarcely any work at all. Indeed, her weakness was so great she could hardly get about. If Mrs. Williams could have eaten heartily and diges- ted her food well, it might be thought she would have recovered. But it was precisely because she could. not do so that the illness came upon her. In other words she was suffering from chronic indigestion and its conse- quences. L'iA her tell her own story. Writing from . her home, 8, Brook-street, Taibach. near Port Talbot, on January 241 h, 1903, she says: "I could riot digest the food I took, and in consequence it lay like lead on mychest, causing me excruciating pain round the heart and between the shoulders, often followed by vomiting. "I varied my diet, ceased to take solids and lived on. bread and milk, but all to no purpose. Loss of sleep, splitting headaches, and flatulency added to my suffer- ings." • _ _ _ .

. The usual means of relief having been tried in vain, Mrs. Williams resorted to Mother Seigel's Syrup, with what result she shall state herself: "After the first two bottles" she declares "I felt somewhat better, but a. marked change took place after I had taken the third. bottle. I could then eat without vomiting or ex- periencing any pain, felemy food was nourishing me, regained strength, and in a short time was quite cured and have never suffered from indigestion since." Truly,no matter what the scales may affirm as to one's weight, one never feels encumbered by it so long as .iplent,.• of well-digested food furnishes the power,. and ftrength which shquld fill it from head to heel. When digestion fails, the remedy—as shown in numberless insta.nces—is the same that restored again to Mrs. Williams the vigour of health.

in his voice showed that he was really terriac4. "That is your own look-out. But you muse stay here until I give you leave to go." "I shall leave Dantbridge when I please !" he cried,. furiously. The old man pointed a menacing finger at him. "You shall do as you are bid," he said, " else I give information to the police. Grant's evidence and what I know about your claim will be enough to justify your aiTes',-, on suspicion of being con- cerned in this crime." •

"Then have me arrested 1" cried Paul, drawing himself up, "and see what will come of it. I can prove my owninnocence, but what of your son?" "My son never killed the man." "How do you know that?" sneered Vane. "He denies it. That is enough for me." "It will not be enough for a jury though. See here, Mr. Hannaford, you leave me alone or I can hang Will. Yes, I can. How, it matters not. You threaten me with arrest. I threaten you with the loss of your son." " l" replied the old, gentleman, quite un- moved by this talk. "I thought you knew some- thing. lam quite willing to run the risk. Will could not well be in a worse plight. If I have you arrested something may come out—in fact, I AITI sure something will come out. 'You make no mistake, Mr. Vane. Move from this hotel until I give you leave or trouble Mrs. Tremewan about your claim and. I have you arrested. Now, you - can take your choice." "I'll do as I please," said Paul sullenly, but much agitated. "Very good. I hope your choice will be to obey. Grant is watching you by my order. If you object you have only to complain to the police. Good day, Mr. Vane," a ndtheold gentle- man walked away: Vane ared'at the clo;Jed door, tht n threw himself into his arm chair where , he stared at the fire and gnawed his nails. The iuterview had ended quite differently to what he expected. Mr. Hannalard walked up the High Street to.. The Gray House, and asked to see Mrs. Tremewan. It appeared that She was in bed very unwell, which was not to be wondered at considering the strain on her at the present time. However, Dora made her appearance, and the old gentleman welcomed her with much affection. The poor girl looked ill and worn. llannaford knew what she must feel after the revelation of Vane, therefore, he was particularly tender towards her. "For Will's sake," said he, and kissed her on the cheek. Poor Dora was so unused to affection that she could make no reply, but utterly broke down. Her nerves were worn thin with trouble. Hannaford quite understood her, and patted on the .shoulder while she wept. "It is all right, my dear," he said; "when you are calmer, I want you to see win."
•- She dried her eyes at once. The name of Will acted like a tonic. "See Will she cried, clasp- ing her hands. "Go to Exeter Prison?"

"Yes. I want you to go to-morrow. I will scom.e to Exeter with you; but you mast see Will, alone. I have an idea, my dear, that this crime in connected with the claim of your cousin "If he is my cousin," said. Dora, growing crimson.

"My dear girl, don't worry yourself over that. For all we know this tale may be a lie. Pillage may be dead. Indeed, I believe he is myself, and that tains story has been invented by Vane to get the. property." "Then if Mr. Pillage is really dead I am "Your mother is legally Mm. Treinewan," said Hannaford ; "that is all right. Vane has yet to prove his case, and between you and me I do not believe he will. I saw him this morning." Here Mr. Hannaford related all that had taken place, and continued. "Now, my dear girl, What I want you, to ido is to see Will and ask him if he caught sight of ,Vane on that night." _ _

"-How: -could he?" asked D-ora, knitting her brows. "lit was dark and rainy." "It is my belief that Vane saw his uncle either before or after Will's visit. In that even Will may—l can't be sure—but he may have seen him. Will is keeping something back even from me and I believe that this something .has to. do with. Vane's presence. Now, Dora, you must make Will tell you all he knows. He must speak out to save himself."
"I rwill do my best," said Dom, clasping the. old man's hand, but lam afraid Will kry. I'll try. I must save him."

div.p: WHAT LOCOMOTOR ATAXY IS

It is a living death. Creeping inch by inch nearer the vital centre of the brain, it lays its victim down incon- stant agony. The first signs are a numbness of the flesh and a tottering of the limbs. This is a symptom which may be taken as a warning. Ileware of it !- Next, the sufferer becomes conscious of a loss of power in the Spine; he is weak and shaken. There are peculiar changes in the eyes. One eyelid droops. The pupil (the dark central spot) of one eye is noticed to be smaller than the other. Soon the patient becomes aware of shooting pains inthe back and limbs—at first slight and transient.

He experiences difficulty in standing steadily: his power of balancing himself erect is gone. At some moment he becomes aware of one of the most peculiar and characteristic signs of the disease: if he closes his oyes while standing, he totters, or may actually fall. IT IS ONLY BY THE AID OF THE EYESIGHT THAT HE CAN BALANCE HIMSELF. The pains grow severer every week, until the agony they cause is indescribable. When the victim lifts a foot to walk, it jerks forward against his will: he can start the Movement but he can't stop it. He can still walk (in a good light) by the aid of a couple of strong sticks—crutches are generally useless. The "lightning pains" (as they are called) increase. Death creeps up the spine by inches, until after agonies too horrible to be described—agonies which make the Perspiration stand in beads on the brow and make a brave man whimper like a beaten child—the inevitable 'end comes; and by this time the sufferer is GLAD TO DIR.

AN EPIEDMIC OF LARCENY AT WARRINGTON.

The Chief Constable informed the magistrates at the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday that there has been aperfect epidemic of larceny in Warrington during the past fortnight, fot the court had scarcely been opened without a case of theft having to be dealt with. Small fines had had little or no deterrent effect. Two more cases were dealt with on Wednesday. In the first a woman named Mary McMiles, last from Preston, was charged with stealing a coat and vest, value 7s. 6d., and another coat and vest value 9s. 6d.. from the shop of Messrs. G. H. and H. E, Jackson, Winwick-street,---It appears that-on Tuesday, Constable Clough, who was on plain clothes duty, met the prisoner in Winwick-street, and noticing something bulky under her shawl, he stopped her. He found her in possession of a new coat and vest, bearing a ticket with Messrs. Jackson's name on it. He took prisoner back to the shop and found that she had taken the goods from the doorway. Clough was informed that there had been a siMilar theft the, previous day, and he discovered that the coat and vest had been pawned by the prisoner who had previously been in the hands of the Preston police for theft at Mr. B, Tyrer's for 3s. 6d.—Prisoner was sent to prison for one month on each charge in the second division.— Mary Cottam, 76, John-street, was then charged with stealing from the shop of Harry Buckley, pawnbroker, Scott-street, on the 14th inst., two pairs of trousers and vests, value 12s. (3d. She pleadel guilty.—The Chief Constahlo stid the goods were missed by Mr. Buckley on the above date, and information was given to the police. It was sabsequeatly discovered that • prisoner had asked a girl named Sewington in Planers-brow whether she was going into Mather's pawnshop, and on being replied to In the affirmative she asked her to pledge a pair of trousers. The girl did so, and gave prisoner the money and .ticket. Subsequently prisoner asked a woman named Tynan to pledge uother pair of trousers at Mr, 13. Tyrer's pawnshop. She refused to give her name, but the trousers were taken in. Mr. Tyrer, who had seen the prisoner outside, re fused to take the clothing unless the woman came inside. Upon this prisoner decamped. Mr. Tyrer kept the trousers and informed the police. Prisoner was an habitual shop- lifter, andas she seldom disposed of the articles herself she was a very dangerous person, as She might cause entirely innocceat persons to 'be arrested for theft, and if they told the bench they had been given the goods by some unknown person the tale would not be be- lieved. She had no need to steal as she had ago od husband and a good home. This was her third appear- ance.—Prisoner was sent to goal for three months. .

The funeral of Mr. Thomas Smithson Routledge, the Market Weighton centenarian, who died un Sunday at the age of 105, took place on Wednesday at Market Weighton. Mr. Routledge spent the -earlier part of his life on the sea, but during the past 40 years he lived a retired life, and spent the last ten years quietly at Market Weighton. He previously lived in Bedfordshire. He stood Gft. high, and had never had a doctor until the last seven months, but.for the last three years he had been nearly blind. Apart. from this he was in possession of all his faculties to the last.

div.head: 'The xam.l
div.p: 'The xam.l
THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE LONDON EDUCATION BILL.

The keenest indignation is expressed amongst Free Churchmen at the provisions of the London Education Bill. It was thought that last year's Act was framed in the worst pos- sible way, but the present bill, whilst contain- ing all the features in the Act of 1902 so objec- tionable to Nonconformists, introduces others which increase the injustice and confusion. All the Progressive bodies in the metropolis are uniting in their opposition to the measure, and in the demand that the education of London— a piece of public work as big as the education of all Scotland—shall be placed in the hands of a body directly elected and directly responsible to the public. The National Free Church Council is entering heartily into the struggle, and a joint committee is being formed repre- sentative of the National Council and the Metropolitan Free Church Federation to organise a campaign of opposition.

div.head: ACT IN THE COUNTRY.
div.p: THE ACT IN THE COUNTRY.

The National Free Church Council is vigi- lantly watching the operations of the Educa- tion Act in the country, and has obtained from the Board of Education an undertaking to furnish the Council with copies of every Interim Report, draft Final Order, and Final Order made under Section II of the Act, which may be issued. These orders will be considered, and action taken where necessary by a Committee consisting of Mr. Robert Whyte, Mr. E. C. Rawlings, Rev. Dr. Clifford, Rev. Thomas Law, Mr. J. Bamford Slack, 8.A., Mr. D. Lloyd George, M.P., and Rev. J. Scott Lidgett, M.A. Every assistance is being affigded to local Councils by the central body, and a letter em- bodying important points of policy in regard to the administration of the Act of 1902 is on the point of being sent out to. secretaries all over the country.
RELIGIOUS INFLUENCES IN THE METROPOLIS.

Considerable controversy has been raised by the publication of Charles Booth's great work on "Life and Labour in London." The third series consisting of seven volumes, deals with "Re- ligious Influences," and Mr. Booth makes some grave charges as to the results, or lack of re- sults, of the operations of the 14arious denomi- nations amongst the poor. Workers who have intimate knowledge, gained by years of labour in their particular spheres, have replied to Mr. Booth's strictures, which in many quarters are felt to be wholly erroneous. But the publica- tion of the volumes will do good if they cause more attention to be directed to the problem of London's toiling masses.

div.head: FREE CHURCH FEDERATION IN AMERICA.
div.p: FREE CHURCH FEDERATION IN AMERICA.

A visit to the United States has been arranged for June and July by the Rev. R. J. Campbell, M.A., tho minister-elect of the City Temple, and the Rev. Thomas Law, the General Secretary of the National Council of the Evangelical Free Churches. Meetings have been arranged in centres all over the States. A National Federation of Churches and Christian Workers is already doing good work, and has recently held its third annual conference; but it was thought that a visit from English Free Church leaders would stimulate the work, and on several occasions invitations have been ex- tended to the Rev. Thomas Law to make a tour of the States for this purpose. There is some doubt at the present time, however, whether the Rev. Thomas Law will be able to leave this country, as arranged, in view of the urgency of the Education campaign.

div.head: AN OPEN-AIR CAMPAIGN.
div.p: AN OPEN-AIR CAMPAIGN.

Now that the summer is almost upon us, arrangements are being made Nr open-air services all over the country in connection with Free Church Councils. Much good work was done in this way last year, in spite of the unseasonable weather, and it is expected that this year greater preparations will be made than ever before. The National Council's Mission Van will probably be at work in Norfolk and Cambridge.

div.head: FREE CHURCH YEAR BOOK.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCH YEAR BOOK.

"The Free Church Year Book and Ocial Re- port" has just been published, and makes a. closely-printed volume of 420 pages. In addi- tion to valuable statistical and other information which makes it a necessity to ministers, secre- taries, and others interested in Free Church work, it includes the• official report of the National Council at Brighton. For the first time are published full verbatim reports of the many valuable and interesting papers, and these will be quietly studied both by those who at- tended the meetings, and the wider Free Church world unable to attend at Brighton. In spite of the increased size, the National Council is issuing the volume at the same price, viz., 2s. 6d. net.

div.head: SITUATIONS FOUND FOR GIRLS.
div.p: SITUATIONS FOUND FOR GIRLS.

A kind friend of the Free Church Girls' Guild has generously undertaken to pay for advertisements of girls connected with the Guilds who require situations. The paper that has been chosen for this purpose is the London Daily News, and arrangements have been made whereby advertisements are received by Guild Secretaries all over the country, inserted, answers received, inquiries made, and negotiations conducted. Un- doubtedly this scheme will provide a long felt want, and its provisions only want to be known to be adopted. Mrs. Charlotte Benham, the Organising Secretary of the Guild, at the Memorial Hall, London, will be pleased to give full information.
NONCONFORMITY IN PARLIAMENT.

Now that matters of vital concern to Free Churchmen are being dealt with by the House of Commons, the article on "Nonconformity in Parliament," by Mr. J. Carvell Williams, ex- M.P., the well-known Vice-President of the Liberation Society, in the Free Church Chronicle, is very timely. Mr. Williams states that it has been calculated that 110 Protestant Noncon- formists were returned at the last General Election. There has been a remarkable change in Nonconformist representation since fifty years ago, when the leaders in. Parliament in the case of Church Rates, &c., were all Churchmen.

"This increased strength of Nonconformity in Parliament," says Mr. Williams, "has had a very material effect in changing the relations of Nonconformists to the Liberal Party as a whole, and to Liberal Governments in par- ticular. I can remember the time when they were regarded by politicians generally as a negligeable quantity, or were made use of for a time and then were flouted or forgotten."
A NIGHT IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Apropos of this, there is a well-written article, illustrated by Harry Furniss, in this month's Free Churchman, on "A Night in the House of Commons," by that well-known Free Church- man, Mr. J. Compton Rickett, M.P. Mr. Rickett recounts the popular conception of life in the House, but points out that to those whose duty it is to legislate the glamour soon wears off, and the work becomes monotonous and trying.

9IPSY SMITH TO VISIT AFRICA. For some time past the Free Church Councils in South Africa have been trying to arrange a visit from Gipsy Smith, the well-known mis- sioner. The Committee of the National Council have at last acceded to the request made, • and the Gipsy is to make a tour to South Africa early next year, probably about March.
