) er. Fri ay, April 24, 1903. THE LATE MR. ROBERT GARNETT, J.P.
REV. JOHN GUNNELL'S TRIBUTE,

On Sunday evening a memorial service to the Lae -31 a. Robert Garnett, J.P., was held in Penketh Wesleyan Chapel and was largely attended. The Rev. John Gunnell officiated, and delivered an impressive address from fife words. "For David, after hehad served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep, and was laid unto his fathers "--Acts xiii. 36. Such in brief was he said, the life and numner of the departure and burial of him in whose memory that tervice was being held. He "served his own generation" faithfully for seventy years, taking as his rule of conduct the "will of God." On the eve of Good Friday he " fell on sleep," passed from us in perfect peace, and on Easter Monday was, byloving hands, " laid unto his fathers" in "sure and certain hope of the resurrection to eternal life." The more notable facts in Mr. Garnett's life might soon be told. Be was born at Vine House, Penketh, on June 6th,1830, was educated at a private school, and in his later youth studied under the guidance of Mr. Slyman, an Anglican clergymen. Hewas apt in acquiring know- ledge, loved learning for its Own sake, and used his mental powers and resources to good prac- tical purpose in after years. He was trained for a commercial life, and at an exceptionally early age developed high business qualities. He set himself to master all the details of his father's trade, and succeeded so well that while yet a young man he was taken into partnership, and on the death of his father in 1877 became the head of the firm, widely known then as now as that of Robert Garnett and Son, cabinet manufac- turers, itc., Warrington. To the extension of thaabusi- ness he devoted the best years of his life, and, by the good providence of God, as he would say, met with a. large measure of success. He did not seek social promi- nence, but gradually drew to himself, as such men ever did, the respect and confidence of the observant and appreciative. His services were soon sought for the furtherance of great public movements for the welfare of the people. Social, educational, and religions objects appealed. to him most strongly,and to these he gave con- stant and cheerful earnest thought, personal efforaand liberal financial aid. A total abstainer himself from very early life, he took the deepestainterest in every phase of the temperance cause, and Was known far and wide as a good temperance worker. The ad- joining day schools, with the erection management, and financial support of which he had so much to do, were evidence enough of the value he attached to the train- ing of the young. Everything that made for the well- being and happiness of his neighbours won his ready sympathy and help. In proof of the esteem in which he was held, and the confidence reposed in his character and judgment, they had only to remind themselves that for nearly 20 years he had been a justice of the peace for the county borough of Warrington, that he had been president of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, member of the Board of Guardians for the Warrington Union, director of the Wesleyan Methodist Trust Aseur- ance Company,member of the Penketh Parish Council, chairman of the Penketh Tanning Company, and had a place on many important committees. It was but the barest justice to say that in all these departments of service he acquitted himself with marked ability, and secured the respect of all with whom he co-opted, and the gratitude of those he served. Into the arena of party politics he rarely if ever entered, but ha might* always be relied on to support the policy which in his judgment in ide for freedom and righteous- ness. In all these matters he proved himself an enlightened christian citizen. But it was with his Christian character and Church work that they had more especially to do .in that service. WIT,t, made him the man he was? What was the master principle of his life ? What was the impelling motivein all this service for his generation? The answer might be given An a single sentence. His conversian was clearly marked. It was in mid youth that he was brought directly under Methodist teaching and influence. His father, whose character and life had such a profound andabiding effect on the son, was led byathe marvellous change wrought in the life of an evil-lifing neighbour on his conversion to seek the Saviour and to join the -Methodist Church. The conversion of a sister of Mr. Garnett's speedily followed, Then the two—the father and daughter— entered into a solemn pledge to pray for the salvation of all the other members of the family. Very soon the Spirit of God was at work in the heart of Robert, who was then on the verge of manhooti. A young friend, a class leader, noted the change in his bearing, and invited him to his class. He went. The step was decisive. Suitable counsel was givext and prayer offered, but the "load of sin" was not then removed. Shortly after, the same witness told there he came from the place of secret prayer with a beaming face, exclaiming "God has pardoned my sins—he has for sure." His name, then placed on the church roll, had been transferred quarter by quarter for more than 50 years without a break. It was there still—such a young man was not likelyt to be a mere nominal member of the church. ill was the day of small and feeble things in Penketh Methodism. But there was work to be done. As in thousands of similar cases the Sunday school was the young convert's first sphere of happy teil for the Master. And as scholar, officer, or occasional teachers, that connection was kept up to the day of his death. How he delighted in the society of children, and how quick they were in spite of a seeming brusqueness of manner, to find out the childlike and kindly heart that was in him. He was seen at his very best in the midst of a group of his grandchildren. For 40 years he was the leader of a society class. He was trustee and trustee's treasurer of this chapel from the formation of the trust in 1860, and to.the several exten- sions and improvements ot chapel and school was a large contributor. In truth he Mid at onetime or other filled every office open to laymen—save one—that of a local preacher. He was a loyal Methodist—well versed in the history and policy of his church, and had strong faith in its power for good in the world owing much to Methodism. He cheerfullyacknovvledged the obliga- tion, and set himself to discharge it. His gifts through the ordinary channels were considerable and constant, and to all appeals for special objects he responded generously. The entire scheme of the Twentieth Cen- tury Fund had his hearty approval, as was evidenced in his noble subscription. But while a devoted Methodist and proud of his church, as every Methodist ought to be, he was no bigot. His outlook, on men and things was wide and sympathetic. He loved good men wherever he met them, and could appreciate good work who ever did it. All through his public life he was a generous friend to all the churches. In his many private benefactions he was always discriminating, but they were never matters of eeetanan preference. He had his limitations, and Hite the rest of them, even the wisest and the best, he made mistakes, though he made fewer than most of them. But how much there was in his life to admire! He was so genuine. They all felt that. Energy of character, strength of will, firmness of purpose he had in abundance, and perhaps he was not altogether free from the defects of these admirable quali- ties ; and they might sometimes have thought him a little harsh in speech and manner. The manifest decay of reverence in recent years was a grief to him. In regular, punctual, and devout attend- anoe on public worship, he was an example to them all. How he revered and loved his Bible. And he had a larger Bible than some of them. His readings was not confined to a few faveurite psalms, and a few striking incidents in the Saviour's life. Much Eastern travel had enabled him to read the Book in the light of Eastern scenes and customs. Few men had a wider or more accurate knowledge of the Old Testament. He was a man of prayer. Long as he was able,ho led the household in daily prayer at the family altar, and about few things -was he more concerned than that every festive gathering of the family should be sanctified by the Word of God, prayer and Christian song. His faith in the providence of God—always strong—view more and more so in the closing years of life. On no topic did he speak more freely and thankfully. His views were broad. He believed in an inclusive—a particular Providence. He did not regard the disap- pointments and losses of life as unfortunate accidents outside the realm of Providence. When some two yeans ago his cabinet works were destroyed by fire, some of them feared that in his enfeebled condition the shock might have serious consequences, but he received the , news in perfect calmness, and NM more concernedabout I the loss to the workmen of the tools than about his own loss of buildings and machinery. His first question was: "Is anyone injured?" Then with the most manifest sincerity he said: "The Lord gave, and the Lord bath taken away: Blessed be the name of tha,Lord." In one . of the public references to Mr. 'Garnett, allusion was ! made to his simple habits. In these days of self-indulg- ence and social rivalry, it was so easy for amen to spend upon himself and his home every penny of his income however large it might be, and in the process lose every- thing worthy the name of happiness. Mr. Garnett spent very little upon himself. His tastes were simple ; and natural. For the beauties of nature he had the I trained eye and the genuine admiration of the artist. . His extensive garden and his beautiful flowers ! were among his chief earthly pleasures. Of ' these he never tired. His kindness of heart had already been referred to, and he only mentioned it that it might rank with the qualities that specially impressed them. The end that all had feared came with startling • suddenness. The very last day was full of pleasant occupation, intercourse with friends,a quiet hour in the conservatory with his New Testament, a gentle walk in the garden among the spring flowers, a short drive into the country—and then the sudden fading of the shadow, and in the deepening twilight our dear friend "fell on sleep." On Easter Monday, in the presence of a vast, , number of friends and neighbours, and with every con- ceivable mark of respect and affection, he was "laid unto his fathers." Letters from all parts of the country had reached the family expressing the deepest ynipathy ; of the writers with them, in their loss and sorrow, and I giving gratifying evidence of the high esteem in which Mr. Garnett was held. Surely there was little need,for him (Mr. Gunnell) to draw any formal lessons. Mr. Garnett's life was full of them; and if they had not discerned them in the course of the narrative and the reading of the testimonies received, it woald be of ! small purpose that special attention should be called ;to them now "He being dead, yet-speaketh." Let two i further words suffice, one, of the dear friend who has

div.head: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
Suggested New Developments.

A meeting of the Warrington Equitable Industrial Society, Ltd., was held on Monday evening. Mr. T. Birchall,.J.P., the president of the Society, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were —Messrs. W. Jeffrey (vice-president), Robert Cook, S. Dunbobbin, E. Williams, Thomas Critchley, Joseph Albinson and Thomas Wadsworth (committee), Mr. A. H. Rathbone (managing secretary), Mr. W. Ford (cashier).

div.head: BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: THE BALANCE SHEET.

The 169th quarterly report and balance sheet for the quarter ending March 30th, showed that the sales were £31,784 13s. 4d.. as against £30,718 55., for the corres- ponding quarter of last year, showing a difference of £1,066 Bs. 4d. in favour of the present quarter. The profits, after, providing for all liabilities, interest on capital, depreciation, &c., will allow a dividend of 3s. in the L on members' purchases.
PROPOSED NEW BRANCH IN THE BEWSEY DISTRICT.

The CHAIRMAN Slid the society was extending its business all along the line. A year ago -they were pay- ing something like £17,000 a year in dividends but now they were paying over .C 20,000 a year. (Hear, hear). A "little while ago Mr. Owen, the society's architect, re- ported to the manager that some freehold property in Bewsey-road was going to be put up by public auction, and the committee could, if they thought fit, have the first option of purchasing it. The negotiations resulted in the _manager securing the property for £720. . .
Mr. HouoiiTos : Where is- ? Mr. JEFFREY: At the corner of Pitt-street

The CHAIRMAN said they were at present being used as residences on of them being occupied by Mr. J. H. Smethurst. The property stood on freehold land, and he (the chairman) considered that the land alone was worth from £2OO to £3OO. With a moderate amount of expenditure, the, properties could be made into good business premises. In a short time Messrs. Greenings works would be started and cottage property in the Bewsey district would be better tenanted. He believed the society would have a good chance of doing a fair amount of business there if they opened a branch in that locality. The last branch which was openedat Stockton Heath was now doing business to the extent of £l4O a week, which for a new business was very good. He thought thesociety might congratulate itself upon acquiring the Bewsey-road properlY at so reasonable an amount.
THE PROPOSED VISIT TO THE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY'S

div.head: WORKS
div.p: WORKS

In answer• to a question by Mr. William Lowe, the Chairman said he did not see how they could arrange fora visit to the Wholesale Society's works, unless 60 or 100 people would guarantee to go. If that number would go the Secretary would make arrangements.
THE AMOUNT ALLOWED FOR DEPRECfATION OF PROPERTY.

Mr. CRO wTH Ea asked if he could be furnished with a statement showing the real value of the Society's property. Year by year the Society had deducted amounts for depreciation, but he did not think the value of the property had depreciated at all. In his opinion it was worth much more than was shown on the balance sheet.

- The CHAIRMAN said it would mean a special valua- tion of the property to prepare the statementasked for. Mr. HAIGH thought the members were entitled to a revaluation of the property so that they might know' exactly how they stood. The CHAIRMAN said the members could rest assured that the property was .much more valuable than was shown on the balance sheet. The members would be glad to know that whatever catastrophe happened in the town, the interests of the members were safeguarded and they would find themselves on the safe side. The SECRETARY said the members might take it for granted that there were very- few co-operative societies in a sounder position than theirs, and no society wail able to give better security. When he first became con- nected with the society 39 years ago,the dividend was 10d. in the 2 but they had been able to pay a dividend of 3s. in the 2 for many years. In some towns there was a disposition to reduce the dividend but in War- rington they were in such a sound position as to be well able to pay 3s. in the £. The CHAIRMAN said he would like to remind the mem- bers that for the-last 30 years the Warrington Co- operative Society had not paid a Jess dividend than 3s. in the X. After some discussion it was decided that the mem- hers should be furnished with the Assessment Com- mittee's valuation of the premises at the next meeting. The report was then adopted. NEW DEVELOPMENTS SUGGESTED. COAL AND BUTCHERS MEAT.

Mr. ELLIS spoke at some length on the advisa- bility of the society establishing a coal siding and delivering coal in small quantities to members. He also expressed the opinion that it would be to the advantage of the society to have a butchering business. He believed a good coal siding could be obtained at Arpley. There were many meln- bers who could not purchase a load of coals at once, and considering that they had 6,000 members, he felt that a good bosmess could be done by supplying coal in bags. Neighbouring societies had also been able to do a good butchering business. Mr. JEFFREY thought the matter might be referred to the Committee. The experience of other co-opera- tive societies had not been very favourable in regard to the butchering business, but he believed they might with advantage have a coal siding. Mr. FARRAR' thought they would be acting wisely in leaving the butchers' business alone, but he quite agreed with the suggestion that a coal business should be started. He moved that the Committee take the matter into consideration and report. Mr. HOUGHTON seconded and thought a coal depot might be established at Fiddler's Ferry for the supply of coal to members at Penketh.
The proposition was unanimously agreed to.

YOUNGER MEN TO BE ADDED TO THE COMMITTEE. Mr. FARRAR said he quite appreciated what had been said with reference to the rapid stlides which the co- 'operative movement had made. The society had been in existence for 42 years and the members entertained the greatest respect for the members of the committee who had served the society for so many years on the committee of management. He was of op ini on,however, that some younger members should be introduced on the committee. The members of the committee were advancing in years and it was absolutely necessary that two or three younger men should be added. The society had over 6,000 members and the business was on the increase. He did not wish to displace any of the members of the committee but he thought it might be enitrged to admit of two or three younger members.
The- SECRETARY said the rules limited the conanitteo •,c) 8 members and a president. _ _ .

Mr. MAYBURY said he believed that if the rples were altered they would have to be re-registered. He agreed with the remarks of Mr. Farrar. The members of the committee had guided the affairs of the society for a long number of years with wlsdom and tact and much of the success attained was due to them. But if they lost two or three of their old members there would be no new members trained in the business, ready to take their places. It would be advantageous to enlarge the committee so that other members might have an oppor- tunity of learning the workings of the society and be able to carry the work on when the older members dropped out of the ranks. The CHAIRMAN said he saw no reason why the num- ber of the committee should not be increased.
Mr. FARRAR then moved that the committee take the matter into consideration and advise the members on what steps to take,to increase the number of committee men.

div.head: PAYMENT OF COMMITTEE MEN.
div.p: THE PAYMENT OF COMMITTEE MEN.

The SECRETARY said it was four years since the com- mittee was granted any remp.neration for their services. He suggested that at the next quarterly meeting the members should grant a sum of ZlO 10s. to each member of the committee as a sort of honorarium for their services. The committee met once a week and some- times twice a week and were not paid for their services. In the past it had been customary to make occasional grants such as he had suggested. .

Mr. MAYBURY said it Wils news to hear that the mem- bers of the committee were not paid for their services. It was high time that the society agreed upon a fixed scale of pay for committee men. (Hear, hear.) It was decided that this matter should be considered by the committee.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
APRIL 24th, 1903.
THE report of the

ENGLISH AND -MOSELEY Commis- AMERICAN WORKMEN. sion will be quoited by employers as evidence of the superiority of the American to the English workman, and by workmen as proof of the inferiority of the English to the American employer. As in most cases, there is a great dea to be said on both sides, and it is all said in the report of the MOSELEY Commission with much candour, force, and incisiveness. Mr. ALFRED MOSELEY, 9,12 employer of labour who was much impressed with the rapid strides made by America as a manufacturing country, induced a number of trade-union officials to accompany him on a tour through the States, to see for themselves how far we are being left behind, and why. This was the "MOSELEY Commission," and the " report " is really a series of reports, from Mr. MOSELEY him- self and from those by whom he was accompanied. In Mr. MOSELEY'S opinion the American work- man is better educated, better fed, better housed, better clothed, and more energetic than his British compeer. He is also "infinitely mora sober." That is enough in itself, surely, to account for the other points of superiority. There are some members of the Com- mission, however, who deny that the American is superior to the English workman. Mr. Cox, of the Associated Iron and Steel workers, maintains that in the iron trades it is the American workman who is the in ferior. So, likewise, says the repre- sentative of the Plasterers. But it is not disputed that the American workman is better off. He gets more wages and lives in higher comfort than a man similarly employed in this country. The employers say that he works harder and produces more. The inducements to work hard are certainly higher than among ourselves. Wages are from 50 to 100 per cent. better than in England ; yet the Ameri- can employer can compete with us for the pos- session of foreign markets, and even in our own. He has beaten us in South Africa, and there are some industries, more particularly connected with electrical development, in whioh he beats us in England. Is this owing to the superiority of the American workmen? The trade union leaders who accompanied Mr. MOSELEY are of opinion that it is owing to the superiority of the American employer. " It is not," says Mr. Cox, "a ques- tion of men, but of methods." If, he adds "British employers will give more attention to elementary methods of manufacture they will be able to shew better results than those now obtained in the United States." This opinion is general among the trade-union representatives. The great employers of labour in the United Stltes are not afraid to throw a machine aside when they have found a better. They do not consider its age. It may have been in use only a few months, but it must go if something more conspicuously labour-saving has been invented. There are, of course, English employers who are enlightened enough to adopt the same policy; but it must be admitted that in a great number of instances they let the old machinery wear itself out, wearing out their own efficiency and their power to compete at the same time. There is a corresponding indictment to be brought against the English workman. He is jealous of machinery. He is apt to regard it as a powerful competitor, and he seldom gets as much out of it as he could. It is admitted Lhat a different spirit prevails among the

workmen of the United States. They welcome new labour-saving machines, because they per- ceive that if the employer profits by them so must they. And this is, in fact, the real cause of the superiority in their condition. It is denied that they are hustlers. They do not work harder than English workmen; but owing to th 3 quahty of their tools and their better surroundings, they produce more. The American printing-offices, says Mr. BOWERMAN, of tho London Society of Compositors, are better equipped in machinery and comfort; therefore they turn out more and better work. That 'is one instance out of many. The general conclusion is that the American system of education is better than our own, that the American employer is more humane, looking after his men's comfort and paying them for any useful ideas they may have to dispose of, and that the American workman has the advantage of working with the best tools and the newest machinery. By emphasising these facts the Moseley report does a real and essential service to the country.

Perusal of the newspapers published in Ceylon to hand by the last mail shows that they have preserved the most "correct" attitude possible in reference to the lamentable death of Sir Hector Macdonald. Without exception they pay tribute to the General's fine qualities and to his services to his King and his country, and they show an excellent example to their home contemporaries in the restraint which they exercise in avoiding discussion of the painful accusations against Sir Hector. But they do not neglect warmly to defend the Governor, Sir West Ridge- way, from the charge that he acted un- sympathetically towards his colleague and subordinate. Ho Never the matter may present itself to the naturally excited minds of the late Sir Hector Macdenald's compatriots, there is no ques- tion that Sir West Ridgeway acted, in a very di cult and painful situation, with courage and wis- dom. He extended his sympathetic advice to the General, and preserved silence as long as it was possible to do so. As soon as it became publicly known that Sir Hector was returning to Ceylon it became impossible to maintain that silence. The General's colleagues en the Legislative Council and the public of the island were entitled to know whether he was returning to resume his post with the charges against him still unheard and unrefuted ; and Sir West Ridge- way had no other course open to him than to con- vey to them the information which, when it was published in Paris, led to the melancholy tragedy which closed Sir Hector's life. Judging from the attitude of the papers, the public of Ceylon has now no other desire than to forget the shadow of those last days in the light of the heroic deeds of the dead warrior on the battlefields of India and Africa,and it is to be hopod that the example thus set,will be taken to heart by those whose excess of zeal would lead to the re-open'ng of a subject which is best left untouched, both for the sake of the living and of the dead.

The property ocrners of Warn i gton have been roused into action by the pending increase of rates. Previous advances in rates have been paid out of the property owners' pockets without affecting the tenants at all, but the rate for educational purposes has proved the last straw, and there is every probability of a general all-round increase in rents. If this does take place' every householder in the town will have brought home to him the cost of carrying °reit the provisions of the new' Education Act. In Warrington it means a heavY rate, and very few will be inclined to commend the Government's action in makurf education a local- instead of a national charge. 'ln a country which professes to give free education, we shall see the spectacle in Warrington in a few weeks time ef the working classes paying increases in rent° ranging from threepence to sixpence per week t° meet the additional rates necessitated by the eevj Education Act. The Act has been unpopular froal the first, but it will be still more 'unpopular when increased rates and rents have to be paid to carry out its provisions.

-1 The members of the Warrington and District Property Owners Association have decided to seek an interview with the Corporation to discuss the situation. The Finance Committee is the proper authority to deal with the question, and in all probability the matter will be referred to that committee. Two suggestions were made by Mr. England which ho thought might be discussed with the Corporation. One htd reference to the composition which the Corporation allow to property owners for collecting the rates fro'l the tenants of cottages, and Mr. England expressed the opinion that they ought to be able to get composition allowed on houses assessed at £l6 instead of £l3. There is nothing to prevent the Corporation from granting a con- cession of this kind to property owners, but it would only benefit a small section and could not be considered as a general concession to property' owners in view of the greatly increased rates. The other suggestion was that the Corporation should be asked to collect the education rate themselves. Tile Corporation are hardly likely to take such a step as this, for the cost of collection would be equal to that of collecting he whole rate from cottagers, for doing which the owners are now being paid a composition equal to one—third of the entire rate. There can be no harm, however, in discussing the question with the Corporation, and some good may come out of the cohference.

div.head: "OUR FOODS." Lecture by Dr. Andrew Wilson.
div.p: "OUR FOODS." Lecture by Dr. Andrew Wilson.

There was a large attendance in the Co-operativo I [all, Sankey-street, an Wednesday evening, on the occa- sion of a lecture by Dr. Andrew Wilson, F.R.S.R. on the subject of "Our Foods." He appeared before them: he said, as the servant of a trust which was spending part of the funds at its disposal in delivering lectures devoted to the exposition of the science of foods. 1.1! referring to the importance of this subject he said it was impossible for us to breed a race of stalwarts unlesg we were well fed. This question lay at the root of our national prosperity. The lecturer quoted with approval the words of Herbert Spencer "The first. essential for success in life is to be a fine animal." if we were to be good citizens; if we were to do our duty by one another ; if we were to do successfully the work that lay at our hand, we must be in good health. We could not be in good health unless we were well fed, and to be well fed was a question of knowing the science of foods, and how the rules of that science might be applied to the conduct of our daily life. TO, Lecturer proceeded to show that our food must consis° of the:same sort of stuff as was found in our body. 135 r a diagram he showed that a man weighing 148 ponndg consisted of 90 pounds of water, 26•61b5. of protein, 23 lbs.of fat, 01 lb. of carbohydrates and 83 of mine' matters. In an interesting way, the Lecturer showee- how the various constituent parts of the body wer2, found in various foods, and he gave the analyse; of many ordinary articles of diet. Milk anui eggs, he showed were important and essentigi foods, and in discussing the value of vegetable° he said they were useful for their mineral properties' The presence of the mineral potash was necessary of keep the blood in order, and it was the absence ee potash in the blood that was generally the cause 0' scurvy and similar diseases. He also dwelt on the necessity of salt and lime being ineluded in the hinune dietary and pointed out that weak limbs were gensrallg attributable to the absence of lime. The lecturer pro; ceeded toldiscuss the relative value of nitrogenous aw: non-nitrogenous foods. Foods, he said, supplied al': wants of the body in several ways. Food furnished tbe, material of which the body was made and also furnish the material to repair the wastes of the body and tt,' protect its tissues from being unduly consumen We consumed food with the further objec'' of producing heat to keep the body warlli„ft and also to produce the muscular and intellecto.- energy for the work which had to be done. He pro. ceeded to show that nitrogenous food went to build u 1;. the body whilst the non-nitrogenous food, or starelia food, supplied the heat and produced muscular °II intellectual energy. It was necessary, he said, to CO bine foods so as to get a propoition of about one nitrogenous to four and a half parts non-nitrogeno d Referring to drinks, the lecturer observed that tea Oot, coffee were not foods but simply stimulants. C°C,. possessed the advantage of being a food as well a'co, stimulant. The lecturer advocated a freer use of as a beverage and pleaded for the support of 13ritp manufacturers as a patriotic duty.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday morning.—Present :—Messrs. J. B. Chad- ick, T. Wright, S. Woodward, J. Knowles, J. Mclntyre wjMosey-Williams, T.Collier, A. Guest, T. Darlington, Spruce, C. E. Linaker, T. Baxter, P. Gleave, J. Mountleld, E. Clarke, J. Bolshaw, J. Whitlow, T. Lewis H. Mawdsley, G. Pilling, E. Bretherton, A. Eaton, T. Antwis, J. Edwards, W. B. Hough, (acting clerk) A. Hulse (actin,, deputy), Dr. Adams (medical officer),W. Dig& and J, Swinton (surveyors), J. Farrington (medical officer). ELECTION OF CEIAIRM Mr. Knowles proposed that Mr. Woodward be appointed chairman of the Rural Council for the ensu- ing year. Mr. Mclntyre seconded and the resolution was una.ni- mously approved. Mr. Woodward in accepting the position thanked the Council for the honour. He could not hope to emulate the deeds of his predecessors but he would do his best.

ELECTION OF VICE-CHAIRMAN. Mr. Spruce proposed, and Mr. Mosely Williams seconded,that Mr. Wright be appointed to the position. Mr. Wright declined to serve. Mr. Edwards suggested that Mr. Stokes be appointed. Mr. Linaker said that it was usual to divide the two offices between the various districts. If they took a chairman odt of Frodsham they ought to take the vice- chairman out of the Budworth district. He suggested that Mr. Pilling be appointed vice-chairman. Mr. Darlington seconded and the motion was xmani- mou.sly passed. THE STANDING COMMITTEES. In considering the composition of the committees,Mr. Edwards objected to Mr. I,inaker being a member of the committee. He did not wish to be personal but he had been chairman of the committee for a year or two and there was a great feeling in Frodsham against him being a member of )he committee at all. The Council unanimously resolved to retain Mr Linaker's name on the committee. It was also resolved that the Highway Committee consist of the council on the motion of Mr. Spruce and Mr. Collier.

A CLAIM AGAINST THE COUNCIL. Mr. H. G. Linaker of Frodsham, wrote claiming £3 10s. damages done to his trap on the 12th instant by the ambulance van running into it. Referred to the Inspector of Nuisances to report on.

THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Adams reported that a case of smallpox had been reported from a Frodsham lodging-house. The con- tacts had been vaccinated and the bedding destroyed. There had been no extension of the disease. The water supply at Moore hospital was not satisfactorY but he thought the supply wouldimprove.

div.head: ESTON ROAD!
div.p: ESTON ROAD!
Mr. Baxter, chairman of the committee, who have the making of the road to Weston, reported that Sandy-lane had been inspected and was in the process of making.
ATTENDANCES.

The following are the attendances for the year out of a possible 26 :—Messrs. Roylance, 19; Greenway, 4; Bolshaw, 12; Knowles, 21; Talbot, 9; Clarke, 26 ; Mclntyre, 14; Whitlow, 9; Stokes, 18; Baxter, 19 ; Linaker, 22; Williams, 16; Lewis, 20; Bradford, 14; Wright, 25; Mawdsley, 16; Collier, 12; Woodward, 22; Ellison, 3; Pilling, 26; Horton, 7; Stokes, 20; Bretherton, 11; Nickson,4 ; Buckley, 7 ; Spruce 18; Eaton, 10; Darlington, 19; Wallington, 6; Mourifield, 18; Turner, 7; Chadwick, 17; Guest, 12; Edwards,l6 ; Darlington, 21; and Williams, 17.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT
EARLESTOWN.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

At the annual meeting of the District Council on 'Monday, the members who had been re-elected made the usual affirmation, as also did the new member, Mr. G. F. Clarke, who after four attempts has at last secured a place on the Council.

Mr. W. Collingwood, was re-elected chairman for the fourth time, after a protest by Dr. Latham. There is a diversity of opinion as to the continued re-election of a particular member as chairman, and doubtless Dr. Latham is one of those who think that a change at times would be beneficial. I don'tsuppose Mr. Coiling- wood would object to retire in favour of a suitable member, but Mr. Ormond, who would out of courtesy be entitled to the position, does not feel well enough in health to take on the onerous duties attached to the post.

The Newton Cricket Club has this week lost a very valuable member, in Mr. NV. Parkes, whose death is chronicled in another column. Though only a young man, the deceased has been a great suffererAndwhilstlhis death affords him relief, his presence will be much missed by a large circle of friends and acquaintances. From a very early age he had been a member of the Cricket Club and a very active one, and last year he was a very popular captain.

div.p: poor rate. If joined to Runcorn he assumed they would have to pay the Runcorn poor rate of 3s. 6d., which would mean a complete rate of 4s. 6d. Several questions were asked by Canon Wood which were answered satisfactorily by Mr. Imison. The pre- I sent rate paid by Weston included a rate for sanitary and other purposes. The 2s. in the pound they paid at present was levied from Dutton. That was the com- plete rate. If Weston were made a part of Runcorn, the overseers wouldlevy only the poor rate proper and in addition the 2s. rate for sanitary purposes. So that the complete rate would not exceed 3s. 3d, to 3s. 6d. in the pound. Canon Wood thanked the deputation for attending and said the question would receive the Parish Council's best consideration. Mr. Handley ta inked the Counoil for affording them an opportunity of conferring together upon the pro- posal.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Annual Meeting. Mr. T. Halton Elected Chairman. Increases of Salaries.
the Council did not consider a mortuary was necesssry No reply had been received from the Local Govern- ment Board.
PK+IKETH DUST CONTRACT.
ST. JOHN'S, EARLESTOW.N..

Mr. E. FOSTER clerk to the Peliketh Parish Council, wrote stating that at the annual parish meeting he was requested to forward the following resolution to the Council :—" That this meeting censures Mr. Pownall, the dust contractor, for the neglectful manner in which he carries out his work."
Mr. KERFOOT said he had interviewed Mr. Pownall, who had given an undertaking that the work would be carried out satisfactorily until the contfact expired.
BURTONWOOD WATER SUPPLY.

Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH, clerk to the Burtonwood Parish Council, wrote enclosing an application which had been forwarded to the authority for the extension of the water supply to four cottages. The main would require to be extended about 150 yards. - The INSPECTOR. was instructed to make inquiries.
PROPOSED EXTENSION OF A SEWAGE MAIN.

The CLERK reported the receipt of a further com- munication stating that at a meeting of Burtonwood ratepayers it was decided that the sewage main should be extended from School-Brow along Clipp's-lane to Green-lane to the point where Green-lane joins Lumber- lane, The consideration of the matter was adjourned for a month.

' The Easter vestry meeting in connection with the above was held in the vestry of the church on Monday evening, the,Rev. T. R. Matthews presiding. Before the business coldmenced Mr. .1. E. Clough proposed a vote of condolence with the Vicar and Mrs. Wilson on the death of Mr:J. Wilson. Dr. Afouncey secondediand the motion was carried, the Vicar briefly responding. Dr. Mbuncey submitted the accounts which showed that the receipts had totalled £271 17s. 19d. including a balance at the commencement of £2l 4s. 11d. The amount in- cluded offertories £129 Os., special collections £7l 16s. sd. and a donation from the Church Building Society of £l5. After meeting all expenses there was a balance in hand of £l6 4s. id. The statement of accounts was passed. Mr. Jones proposed the election of Mr. T. A. Pimblett as people's warden. This was seconded and carried. Dr. C. J. Mouncey was elected vicar's warden. The following were elected parishioner's sides-men : Messrs. Duncan, Rylance, Jones, Clayton, Dean and Tialby and Messrs. Boardman, Dale, J. E. Clough, Hackett, Hemmings and Taylor as vicar's sidesmen. Dr. Monncey proposed that a voluntary rate of 2d. in the £- be levied as usual. This was seconded and agreed to. Mr. Anderton proposed a vote of thanks to the choir and organist and referred to the splendid work accomplished in this department. This was carried. The Vicar referred to the recent fire at Neu-church Parish Church and said that he was of opinion that the church ought to be insured heavier than it was. Votes of thanks to the Vicar and the officials of the church concluded the meeting. ST. PETER'S, NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS.

The vestry meeting in connection with the above was held in the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Monday evening. The Rev. J. Ryder presided over a small attendance, the new curate (Rev: J. Le Moine) being present. Mr. W. H. Hindley presented thestatement of accounts which showed that the receipts had been £l5l Bs. 11d. including a balance brought forward of £29 18s. 11d, subscriptions amounting to £B2 us. 3d. Seat rents £25 and collections £l6 7s. 3d. After pay- ing all expenses a balance of £3l 16s. 3d. was.left at the bank. The statement was approved. Owing to the death of Mr. Parks the statement had only been certi- fied by one auditor but this was deemed sufficient under the circumstances. A vote of condolence with the family of the late Dr. J. W. Watkins who for 40 years was an active worker in connection with the church, was passed and also one to Mrs. Pa.rkes,and the family of the late Mrs. Smith, of Brookside. Mr.J. Sankey was elected vicar's warden and Mr. W. H. Hindley people's warden. The following were, elected Vicar's sidesmen : Messrs. J. St. Leger, C. Cole, J. Singleton, S. Twiss,and. Messrs. T. Ritchie, P. Percival T. Mayor and J. W. Austin as parishioners' sidestnen. Messrs. J. Liptrott, jun., and R. W. Wilkinson were elected auditors. Votes of thanks were passed to all the workers, Mr. J. Sankey responding. The Vicar announced that in response to numerous applications he had decided to commence Sunday morning service at . 11 o'clock instead of 10.45 as hitherto. This would be Itried for 12 months and if it did net prove suitable they would revert to the old method.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. SEPTITON reported that during the month there had been 23 births and 28 deaths. The death-rate was equal to 304 per 1,000 against 32 the average for the corresponding month last year. Fifteen deaths occurred in the County Asylum at Winwick and exclusive of these the death-rate was 14'1 per 1,000.

div.head: GRANTS FROM THY: COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: GRANTS FROM THY: COUNTY COUNCIL.
The SURVEYOR reported that the County Council had granted £lOO towards the macadamising of Cinamon- lane, and £5O towards the macadamising of Glazebrook- lane, Padgate.

div.head: VULCAN BRIDGE.
div.p: VULCAN BRIDGE.

The SURVEYOa reported upon improvements which had been made at this bridge and stated that traffic was resumed on Wednesday the Bth. inst. The bridge and the retaining wall were now all as good as new, and the retaining wall was set in the new line, so that when the bridge was widened none of the present work would need to be rehandled.

div.head: WINWICK ASYLUM ENTRANCE.
div.p: WINWICK ASYLUM ENTRANCE.

The SURVEYOR informed the Council that the work of lowering the entrance to Winwick Asylum to the levels of Pennington's-lane had now been completed, the gates dropped twenty inches and he thought the approach to Pennington's-lane, would be better than previous to the obstruction.
THE SURVEYOR APPLIES FOR AN INCREASE'OF SALARY

Having represented his report,the Surveyor submitted an application for an increase of salary.. He stated that he had now been with the Council as Surveyor three years and including the time served with the-late Surveyor for a total period of over eleven years. During the last three years the work of the Council had increased very considerably, in fact an inspection of the account books and ledger, compared with the old ones would.he ven- tured to think, be a surprise to many both as regarded Ithe amount of extra detailnow gives, the larger amount • of work carried out, and general expenditure. The County improvements had much more than doubled and he thought they would go on increasing. This, coupled with the largely increased secondary rates, was but an , instance showing that the County authority was recog- nizing the rapidly growing importance of the district apart from the increased improvements (County and otherwise) which all required survey, sections and general carrying out. The detail and routine work was' also growing and he ventured to say was getting into good ship-shape methods and systems which had been changed entirely during the last three years. The sur- veyor pointed out that hs present salary was £l6O as against .2400 paid to the late surveyor. The commission earned from the County this year would be more than 2180 actually paid to the. Council's account, so that it would readily be seen that his present salary was more than covered out of County maintenance. There WtCS also au actual perman- ent relief to the rates by the district roads being promoted to secondary, and though making more work for the officials, at the same time they were able to show a re- duction of the rate for the coming half year. Mr. IVIATHER. gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that Mr. Newcombe's salary be increased to £2OO. Mr. BROOKS seconded.
The CLERK said Mr. Neweombe's work was very high class, and he was improving in his knowledge every yelr.
Mr. HALTos :
I think so too.
Nt. KNawLEs said that lately he had felt very highly satisfied with the work in the Surveyor's department. The meeting then concluded.

div.head: FARMER AND HIS LAWYER'S BILL.
div.p: A FARMER AND HIS LAWYER'S BILL.
" A Daar Luxury."
ST. JAMES', LATCHFORD.
The anmml vestry meeting was held in the schools on Monday evening, the Vicar (Rev. F. R. Pearson) pre- siding. There was a fair attendance..
ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The Vicar; in nominating Mr. H. N. Houghton as his warden, thanked that gentleman, for the kindness he had shown him since he had been in the parish, and for the uniform way in which he had encouraged and backed him up in all his efforts. Mr. William Eckersley was re-elected people's warden, on the proposition of ,Mr. Astley, seconded by Mr. Morris, and supported by Mr. Houghton. Alderman Hutchinson was -nominated as Mr. Houghton's sidesman, and Mr. -Utley as Mr. Eckersley's sidesman.
The Vicar expressed his gratitude for the help and sympathy given to him, and trusted ,that their working might be as harmonious in the future as in the past.
THE, ACCOUNTS,

Mr. Houghton submitted the statement of accounts, which was adopted. Thetotal income was £159 19s. lid., including general collections £32 Os. 11d., and special collections £4B Os 2d., while the expenditure amounted to £l7l Os. Bd. There was a deficit of £ll Os. 9d, as against 2-1 6sa sd. at the commencement of the year. LAY
-REPRE,SENTATIVES AND SIDESMEN.

Messrs. Houghton and Burgess were re-appointed lay representatives on the motion of Mr. Stansfleld, seconded by Alderman Hutchinson ; and Messrs. Acton, -Fargher, Morris, Tonge, Rathbone end Hill were elected sidesmen, on the proposition a Mr. C. S. Burgess, seconded by Mr. Stansfield. • • SERVICES TEMPORARILY ..ABAI6ONED.

The Vicar announced his intention of dropping cer- tain week-day services until he was able to obtain another curate, because no man could do more than his health or strength would permit. He thanked his people sincerely for their continued sympathy with him in his sore trial, and, for their kindness and forbearance in many ways which he could not refer to for one moment at a public meeting. He also thanked all the workers of St. James', and he was proud that they were too • numerom for him to profess iii any way to mention by name. Never in any parish had he found such quiet, unostentatious work for Uod without the slightest hope of fee or reward as had been done in that parish,and he asked their people to be really true to their honourable traditions.- .
A vote of thanks was accorded to the Vicar for pre- siding.
CHRIST CHURCH. LATCHFORD.
The Vicar (Rev. F: Screeton) presided at the Easter vestry meeting in connection with Christ Church, Latchford, which was held in the Parish Schools, Wash-lane, on Saturday evening.

STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS. Mr. John Fairclough (the Grange) made a statement with reference to the accounts of the wardens. He said they commenced the year with.a balance of £3 4s. 21d. in hand, and they left off with a balance in their favour of £2 us. id. The offertories had been larger this year than ever in the history of the church. The total amount received was £316 18s. 9d. The sum of £43 Bs. 3d. was raised for the hospital, and £24 2s. 6d. for the church enlargement, while the Easter offerings for the Vicar mine to <£Bl 17s. Bd. (Applause.) The general offertories for the Church had been £l6O 4s. 9d.. The accounts were adopted. • APPOINTMENT OP OFFICERS.

The Vicar appointed Mr. John Fairclough J.P. as his warden. • Mr. Longhottom was elected people's warden, Mr. Dakin having expressed a wish to retire. Messrs. Bernard Tinsley, Lowe, Plevin, Margetts and Dakin were appointed sidemen, and Messrs. Lowe, and Dakin, lay representatives. -

div.head: INCREASE Or THE ENDOWMENT.
div.p: INCREASE Or THE ENDOWMENT.

The Vicai-C--1;t:i:ila-ted-the wardens on the excellent results which had been pat before the meeting. The chief event of the year had been the enlargement of the church, which would accommodate 100 more people. The work had been done at a cost of £1,330 or a little more, and every penny of the money had been paid— hear, hear)—in fact they had a small balance in hand, namely £3 18s. The Vicar alluded to the gener- osity of the people in raising so much money each year, and thanked the congregation for their , extremely generous offerings on Easter Day. The. sum amounted to close upon £B2 and was the largest offertory on Easter Day in the history, of the church. He regarded such generosity as, a kindly expression of goodwill and confidence; it was a very tangible ex- pression of the feeling of the people towards him. The living was one of the smallest in the district ; he did not know whether it was not the smallest. The endow- ment up to the present time had been only £BO a year- -250 from Grappenhall tithes and-230 from the, Eccles- iastical Commissioners. But the endowment had been increased, and from the Ist August next, instead of being £BO it would be £92;'o tirat he would now be able to go a few miles further on his summer holidays. (Laughter). That state of things was tha result of the process he mentioned at the last Easter vestry meeting —that if £lOO was offered to the living it would in ordinary cases be met by the diocesan institutions by making it into £2OO. If they gave an equal sum, the Ecclesiastical Commissioners would double it. But that was not the whole that was likely to happen. He did not think he would be doing wrong in disclosing what Mr. Dakin's intentions were with regard to the matter las he had generously offered another £lOO (Applause) Unfortunately these things moved rather slowly. Mr. Dakin"s , £lOO had been offered the diocesan institutions. He would not have theira.nswer for some time,and after receiving it he would have to write to the Commis- sioners to tell them that £2OO could be offered to the living. He would not receive their reply until next March. Of course Mr. Dakin would not give the £lOO • unless his offer was met in the usual way. Mr. Screeton , added that the number of communicants on Easter Day was 383, about three times as many as three years ago, or one-seventh of the population of the parish. He thought they might congratulate themselves on the _ I healthy condition of their church work. ,
VOTES OF THANKS,

Hearty votes of thanks were accorded to the retiring officers; the lady church workers (who raised £383 in aid of the church enlargement); to Mr. Bernard, the treasurer of the day schools; to the ladies who had decorated the church on Easter Day and on other occasions; to the auditor; and the choir, Mr. Long- bottom observing that few chnrches in the district had a more beautiful service or a more efficient choir. The , service on Good Friday evening was a source of pleasure to all. Several of the parishioners present spoke in high praise of the choir. The Vicar was thanked for presiding.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Leh-street Primitive Methodist Church.

On Sunday last the Sunday school anniversary ser- mons were preached by Mr. Hartshorne of Darlaston. The church was tilled at' each service, and the congre- gation thoroughly enjoyed the two discourses of Mr. Hartshorne at the morning and evening services. The morning voluntaries were "Andante con Moto," Smart, and "Grand March," Hill. Appropriate hymns foi the occasion were sung by the choir and children, and the one entitled " Christ shall lead us" was excellently well renclorst In the afternoon a musical service was held, Councillor James Dodds presiding. The following was the programme :—"Solo, "The Holy City" by Mr. Roberts ; solo, "The Lost Chord" by Miss L. Hayward; violin solo, "Romanza," Mr. A. Bennett; hymn by the children and choir, " Christ shall lead us"; song. "The King of Love" by Miss A. Bridge; song, "The Heavenly Rest" by Mr. Roberts; violin solo. "Nocturne" Mr. A. Bennett; solo "Children of the city" by Miss A. Bridge; song "The Vesper hymn" by Miss Hayward; chorus, "Hallelujah "' from the f` Messiah ' ; organ solo" Festal March in" G" Smart. Each item was heartily appreciated. At the evening services Miss L. Hewitt and Miss Elsie Spruce sang a duet. The choir rendered in theirlusually fulished manner the choral march entitled" Warriors of the Lord," and gave a fine interpretation. The organist contributed "Festive March" by Fa.ulkes, and " Adagio " and " Allegro " from Second Organ Concerto by Handel. The collections amounted to the excellent sum of £l4, being greatly in advance of previous years. Mr. Albert Spruce ably conducted and Mr. Fred Podmore presided at the organ in his usually accomplished manner.

div.head: Baptist Church, Colborne-street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Colborne-street.

On Sunday last, at the above church, sermons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. J. S. Hughes. of Hill Cliffe. The subject of his evening dis- course was entitled "Js life worth living ?" Four aspects of life commonly taken by men at the present day were touched upon,and it was shown that none who held these view 4--, could find happiness and satisfaction. Only the Christian life, the preacher pointed out, the life lived to noble purpose, and to the glory of God, could truly be e tiled " worth living."

div.head: Ellesmera-street Wesleyan Methodist
div.p: Ellesmera-street Wesleyan Methodist
Mission.

An anniversary service was held in this Mission on Sunday, when Mr. G. W. Littler, of Runcorn (formerly of Warrington), preached from the text "Where hast thou gleaned to-day ?" During the service an anthem was rendered by the choir, under the leadership of Mr H. Llewellyn, Mr. J. Hulse officiating as organist. There was a largecongrogation, and the offertory was in aid of the trust funds.

div.head: Congregational Church, Newton.
div.p: Congregational Church, Newton.

Special services in connection with the anniversary of the Congregational Sunday school, were held in the above Church on Sunday. Beautiful weather prevailed, and there was consequently large congregations at each of the services, especially inthe evening. The pulpit at the morning and evening services was occupied by the Rev. Hugh C. Wallace, of Bristol, who gained notoriety as a povrerful exponent of the Gospel, durfng his visit to F.arlestown on the occasion of the shmultaneous mis- is, two years ago. His discourse in the morning was selected from the subject "Why am I a Christian,' and was excellently delivered. The subject of his evening discourse was Why am_ I a Congregationalist ?" In

the treatment of this before a mix-ed -congregation, he (mused great offence, by his ill-timed reference to the Anglican Church and the Roman Catholics.—ln the afternoon a cantata entitled " Moses " was given by the choir and children, and was very well rendered, Mr. D. R. Owen presiding at the organ.—The collections throughout the day amounted to over £57.

The wealthy lottery organiser Albert Adams, known as the Policy King of New York, has been convicted of keeping .7. bettin,, establishment and sentenced to a year's imprisonment. The Rev. W. B. Melville, minister of the West Free Church, Bushby, Lanark, was knocked down and killed on Wednesday afternoon at Eglington-street Station, Ghogow, while crossing from one platform to another. He was about GO years of age.

WOMEN'S CHAT.

The arrangements for the visit of the King and Queen to Scotland next month, are to permit of their Majes- ties being present at the opening of the Royal Military Tournament, which is always one of the most popular shows of the London season. Its special feature this year in the form of a pageant., will be the representation of the proclamation Durbar at Delhi. It is to be a very realistic representation, and will comprise repre- sentatives of the Indian Princes, and the principal British and Indian regiments which figured in the great spectacle. The musical ride, which is a regular feature of the tournament, will,in the first week, be entrusted to the 2nd Life Guards, and in the 2nd week to the sth Lancers, who with Bugler Dunne sounding the charge, so greatly distinguished themselves at Elandslaagate,the first British victory in the late war. Dalkeith Palace, where the King and Queen are to reside during their visit to Scotland, is being thoroughly, done up and redecorated. The building is not particu- larly attractive in its exterior, but it has many fine apartments and some idea of the expense involved upon the Duke of Buccleuch by the Royal visit may be gathered from the fact that some thirty or forty of the rooms are being entirely refurnished. This is always done in the Royal apartments, whenever the King and Queen are the guests of any of his Majesty's subjects, but Dalkeith Palace is being practically refurnished throughout. Large as it is, it is not likely that the accommodation will prove adequate, and in that case some of the officers of the suite will probably stay at Newbattle Abbey, whilst others will have rooms at one of the leading hotels in Edinburgh. The Prince and Princess of %Vales have been able to occupy Marlborough House earlier than was expected, in view of the extensive repairs and alterations that have been carried out at the former residence of the King and Queen. It is a much larger mansion than York House, which has now become the London resi- dence of Prince and Princess Charles of Denmark. There will be a garden party at Marlborough House during the season, and it is probable that, with more ample accommodation, the Prince and Princess of Wales will entertain on a larger scale than formerly. After this year the number of pictures that may be sent to the Royal Academy by outsiders will be limited to two, whilst Academicians wll be limited to six, in- stead of eight. This rule will be of more consequence to women artistes than to men, since they are not ad- mitted as Associates, and therefore though the merit of their paintings may be of the highest order, none can send up more than two pictures to go before the Selec- tion Committee. The Academicians and Associates have the first call and out of all the thousands sent up, there is only room for ten to twelve hundred. There ' is no just cause why women artists should be handi- capped in this way. They have been admitted to the Villa Medicis, the famous art school in Rome. and women artists ought to be admitted to the full privileges of associates of the Royal Academy. The choosing of a motto either for decorative pur- poses, or as an ideal to live up to, has become quite a popular craze among fashionable women. That belong- ing to the family coat-of-arms is not always the most suitable,though it is in some instances, as in the case of Earl Sondes, 'Be what you seem." That would make an excellent motto for all women, but as a rule, the motto of the family crest is hardly the most appropriate to women's idea, nor is this surprising when we con- sider that many of them date back to a period when women were not thought to be of much account. Hay- ' ing made her own special selection, the fair mottoist proceeds to have it inscribed on her note paper, and embroidered on her handkerchiefs, and so on,—and if the motto is one that may be made a test of her daily life, ,it may even serve a still better purpose than that of a pretty decoration. When indulging in a new gown a yard or two of the fabric of which it is built should, when possible, be secured. At the present time, such an investment is of the greatest service, in bringing lastoyears sleeves up to date. These should be slashed open, extra pieces inserted, and the joins hidden beneath insertions of lace, or bands of embroidery, when it is impossible to detect such a renovation. Nothing dates like the sleeve, and the possibility of having to provide new, should be provided for whenever possible. Among other useful accessories, which an extra length of fabric matching a gown renders possible just now,are an early Victorian tippet, or a dainty covering, consist- ing of four or five little highwayman capes, one above the other, with a wide strap of velvet by way of collar, fastening over on one side. These graceful wraps afford a certain amount of warmth, yet can easily be discarded when desirable. _ _

With regard to shape in headgear, it would seem as ' though nothing further is demanded than that it may be artistic; and becoming to the face of the wearer. The very widest latitude is allowed, and the woman who dons an unbecoming hat or toque deserves little in the way of sympathy. At the leading milliners no two shapes will be found to be alike, all such firms build their own, curving and twisting to suit the require- ments of each customer. Only women possessed of a goodly dress allowance can, of course, go to such estab- lishments for their headgear, but lesser lights are now m eking efforts in the same direction, often altering the shape and arranging the trimmings upon the head, then studying the whole creation from every point of view.. The leading millinery colour just now is green, in those delicate shades which are most becoming to young and clear complexions. The bright spring sunshine has an unpleasant knack of showing up the ravages of time, and furniture, hang- ings and carpets that appeared in fairly good condition during the dark days, often cause the housewife many qualms at this season of the year. In the matter of ' carpets, much can be done by ripping up seams, and turning sides to middle, or a shabby breadth to that part of the room where it will not be seen. After beat- ing, and sweeping, a hard rubbing over with flannels wrung out of water, in which a little ox gall has been stirred, is the best possible process, the carpets being hung in the open air until dry, when the colours will be found to be wonderfully bright and clear. For shabby leather, white of egg, lightly applied then well rubbed off, is an excellent restorer," so also is a mix- ture of one-third of vinegar, and two-thirds linseed oil, boiled up together. This should be allowed to get cold before using, and be very sparingly rubbed in. The prosecution of a nursemaid at Westminster sug- gests the reflection that bassinettes and perambulators are placed in rather a difficult position. The com- plainant in this case contended that the ybung woman had no right to wheel the bassinette on the footway, and probably he was right. Bassinettes on a footing are apt to be a nuisance,and no doubt many people have had the same experience as the complainant without going to the trouble of taking out a summons. If on i the other hand, the bassinette s wheeled in the road it is pretty sure to'be run into sooner or later, by a motor car, a horse and cart, or an inexpert cyclist to any nothing of the emphatic comments of some drivers,who think that bassinettes have no right to be in the road- way. _ _
MADGE.

N.S.P.C.C. Work. During the quarter ended 31st March, the Warring- ton and District Branch of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (Local Office,34 Parker-street,Warrington),inquired into 82 complaints, of which 80 cases were found to be true, and affected the welfare of 204 children. There were 110 offenders. Action was taken as follows :-.—Warnings were given in 66 cases ; 2 cases were dealt with by transfer, &c., and 12 cases were found to be of such a gross nature as to necessitate prosecution. One year eight months of imprisonment with hard labour, was imposed and six defendants were bound over to come up for judg- ment, &c. The Society's Inspector made 326 visits of supervision ; three of the children died, before or during inquiry.

The Rev. A. N. Taylor's Departure. The Rev. A. N. Taylor, curate of St...lanies' Church, Latchford, has left Warrington in order to take up a similar appointment at St. Mary's-without-the-Walls Church, Chester. The Vicar (Rev. F. R. Pearson) paid a tribute to Mr. Taylor's good work in the parish on Monday evening at St. James' annual- vestry meet- ing. He observed that he had had many curates, but he could honestly say that he had never had one for whom he had a greater regard than Mr. Taylor. Never in his life had he came 'across a man who was more consistently devout, and who put more con- science in what he believed to be his work. Although he had only known Mr. Taylor a few months, an acquaintance had ripened into a friendship, and a friendship had ripened into an affection that death could only sever. In his own name and in the, name of the congregation he hoped that God's blessing might be with him wherever he might happen to be ' A Local Parish Church Burnt. The ancient Parish Church of Newchurch, near ro ft, was almost totally destroyed by fire on Sunday morning. The fire had already btamed a good hold when it was discovered, and although the Glazebary Mill Brigade were quickly in attendance they had to devote Themselves mainly to shying the tower and belfry. • In this they were successfa and the parish registers and communion plate were rescued from the flames. The roof of the main building, however, fell ! in with a loud crash, and a portion Of the walls gave . . wav, the church being almost completely gutted. The new organ and stained-glass windows to the memory ' of Bishops Wilson and Dr. Black, former rectors Of the parish, were -destroyed. The edifice at Newchurch is closely connected with Cromwell's coming into Lancashire, for it was there that the notorious Colonel Blood, who attempted to steal the crown jewels from the tower of London, was married to a Maria Hol- croft, a village young lady. The loss., which is estim- ated at £3,500,, is only partially covered by insurance. llt is not known how the -fire originated, but it is sup- posed that the heating apparatus was at fault.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

There are a great variety of very charming trimmings used on this season's gowns, and these range from old laces to every variety of passementerie and embroidery. Many of these forms of trimming are of great assist- ance to the home worker, as quite a simply made toilet can be rendered very smart by the addition of one or even two varieties. Old brocades which have been up to now considered useless will, when showing a floral pattern cut up nicely into medallions, which can be used to trim cloth dresses, arranged round the lower part of the skirt in graduated circles framed as it were in wreaths of guipure or narrow lace. Some of the newest

div.head: PRBTTY COSTUME,
div.p: A PRBTTY COSTUME,

embroideries are very weighty in consequence of -the different materials used In their em- bellishment, and the patterns are for the most part large and effective; while the colours are rich, this gorgeousness being em- phasised by the gold and .silver thread with which they are often picked out: There are also some very beautiful and also durable raised sprays and garlands of flowers made in a particular kind— of tissue, which very closely imitate the real blossoms. The pretty costume sketched is of pale -biscuit coloured voile trimmed with a floral patterned passe- menterie in delicate brown and pink. A neck band of pink crêpe de chine and -a_ folded waistband en suite complete a costume which though simple is yet elegant enough to be worn on any occasion. There are some truly elegant cloth gowns displayed among the best and latest models trimmed with linen embroideries and guipures, while the smartest linen or other washing dresses and blouses have coloured linen galons worked with ,a pattern in flourishing thread applied in different ways, such as mitred strappings, or for outlining the collar and cuffs., or the 'stole-like fronts.
V IMMO, -

div.head: DAINTY BLOUSBi
div.p: A DAINTY BLOUSBi

Black and white lace makes a pretty trim- ming for summer toilettes, especially the dainty coloured cotton and muslin dresses. Indeed, nearly, all the most successful light dresses still show a touch of black introduced very lightly into their construction, either in the lace trimmings or in the -finishing touches at neck or waist. Several of the newest laces of the moment have painted or em- broidered medallions let into them, but these are of a very costly description and are therefore confined to the adornment of the more expensive gowns.

The dainty blouse depicted is of cream silk and lace and is very smart in design. Blouses are as numerous nd as much worn as ever, and are of infinite variety. For morning wear there is the simple tucked shirt blouse completed at the throat by a tine lawn and lace collar, and a silk cravat with the ends embroidered in coloured silks. The aftenioon blouse is of silk or crepe de chine with lace or embroidery liberally introduced, while - the evening blouses are of the most elaborate description, with all sorts of delicate and rich fabrics intermingled with the most charming effect. It takes a considerable

div.head: MORNING TOILETTE:
div.p: A MORNING TOILETTE:
amount of natural good taste and long training to arrive at a judicious result, as all overtrimmed effect would otherwise mar the tout ensemble.

Sleeves are becoming very voluminous below the elbow, and, indeed, the tendency is rather to exaggerate this effect in an undesirable fashion. The upper part of the sleeve is tucked or drawn closely so as to fit the arm perfectly, while the fulness springs out below the curve of the elbow. In spite of the fact that this mode is in vogue it must be confessed that the ample folds of material round the lower part of the arm are rather apt to be in the way and hinder the free move ment of the wrist and hand.

The smart coat and skirt shown in my illustration are made of grey canvas flecked with white, with narrow stitched bands of emerald green silk and small tassels of the same colour. The loose coat fits the figure neatly in spite of its easy character, and the skirt, which like the coat is lined with green silk, has strappings finished with oxidyzed nuttons, smaller, but of the same design as those which fasten the coat. It is worn with a straw hat of a burnt shade, trimmed with bright green rosettes, and a quill laid flat across the crown. The little shoulder capes give a very smart effect to the figure. The skirt is of a convenient walking length. The short skirts are in many instances drawn into a shaped band or empiecement round the hips, but there are some materials which do not lend themselves readily to drawingJ Sometimes the fulness is kept down by strappings, as in this way any over fulness at the hips te prevented loialls4llll,-* - - COMMA

div.head: RAILWAY,
div.p: RAILWAY,
THE NEW MOTOR-COACH NOW RUNNIN
A RAILWAY MOTOR-COACR.

In the railway world the latest novelty is a motor-coach, which is running on the London and South-Western Railway, between Havant and Fratton. It contains two compartments for passengers—first - class and third. In the first-class compartment the seats are arranged longitudinally, and there is accommodation for ten people. The third-class compartment is built f9r thirty-two passengers. The seats are arranged in pairs transversely on either side of a gangway down the centre. The coach thus carries forty-two passengers all told— which is about the number you may some- times see distributed throughout a long train during slack 'r -ours. The passengers can enter at either end by means of little platforms fitted with sliding gates, like the platforms of trams: The little compartment in front of the main body of the coach is intended for luggage. The engine looks small, but it is wonderfully compact, and quite powerful enough for the work required of it. A technical description of its construction would not appeal to the lay reader, but it may be said that it can get up a speed of thirty miles an hour in thirty seconds from starting, a feat which is far beyond the ordinary full-grown engine: The ordinary passenger engine can only reach twenty miles an hour in thirty seconds, so that the motor-coach will have a great advantage over a train on routes where stations are frq- quent.

has been outgrown by the enoimOus increase in this business, was so called after an old coffee-house, which previously occupied the 3ite ; but the new building is more likely to be called the Shipping Exchange, as the signi- ficance of the other has long since been lost in time. Hithertd at the Baltic, and now at the new exchange, all the broking in connec- tion with shipping has been 'done, just as. stocks and shares are dealt in on the Stock Exchange. Ship-broking has by degrees become a highly important • feature of the trade, and causes a great deal of speculation. It has many branches and is a great and in- tricate business by itself, but it must not be
confused with Lloyds; as is sometimes the case. The new -building is another additiou worthy of the great .capital of the Empire.

div.head: RECORD CUP TIE.
div.p: THE RECORD CUP TIE.

Saturday's cup-tie was truly a record. No team has scored such simple goals as did Bury, but apart from this they were much the better team, and Derby cannot point to Fryer's absence 'as a reason for their defeat, for before he retired Bury had won the match. George Ross, the veteran skip- per, appropriately opened the scoring. A lot of people seemed to put that goal down as a sort of fluke. Ross's 'shot was, however, a good one, and fully deserved a goal. The best of the lot was that of Plant's. The ball was touched in to him by Sagar, and after gathering himself, Plant, still one of our best extreme lefts, crashed it through with his right foot. It was a grand goal. About the other points which made up the half dozen, it is not necessary to say a great deal, except that while they were more or less lucky, on the run of the play they were tho- roughly deserved. Bury were immeasurably the better team. There was not a single
MR. J. ADAMS (RruFEREE).
