div.p: DERBY CO. CAP CAIN

position in the field in v.l).ch they did not excel. • Monteith had not more than eight or nine shots to stop during the whole afternoon, but he !lasi a couple of warm customers during tl last twenty-minutes, when the sole effort.> of the Bury side were devoted to the emulaCoA of Preston North End's performance n 1889—winning the Cup without having a goal scored against them. But tins year's performance of Ilurv's is decid.Aly in front of that of N orth End, for tiwy have met much better 1, alas. The men .say that the hardest match tv have ha: was ai.ainst I,Volverhampton ;:iclerers, in the f rst round. The Bury

record this year is, 17 the way, somewhat peculiar. The trst I hree rounds they won by —0 in each ca:ie : in the semi-final against Aston Vi!la they exactly doubled the aggr,..ga te .score by winning by 3-0 : while in the final they aga ill doubled the semi-final score, winning be 6--o. They have thus scored -12-0 in the series of Cup-ties, and are naturally very proud of it.
AN ILL!CIT STILL. IN LONDON.

Quite unconinion in:ly be said to b.: the case-in which Arthur White and Janet Dud- ley figure as dekndants. They are charged with manufacturing exciieable liquors in an unaccustomed p!ace, at 34, Turner Square, I-lox- ton. The Excise autliol.ities raided the place and- found an extensive and complete distil- ling plant, together with 'several gallons of spirit of an illicit ehardcter. The still is in some stables in one of the most populous parts of lioxton. The stables were formerly used by the Hoxton ,Brewery Company, and the name of that firm still remains on the large gates. It is not until one gets inside the gates and closes them that one notices how well adapted they are for the purpose to which they have been put. The small stableyard fs not overlooked in any way ; not a single window can be seen in any of the adjoining LEY..
THE HOXTUN U LICIT STILL

houses, and, therefore, when Once the stable doors were closed, the occupants of the place were never in clanger of being seen by any- one. The still itself is a great improve- ment on the ordinary illicit still. It has evidently been erected by someone possessed of expert.knowiedge, and it i,s cap- able of making a very clear, good spirit, forty overproof. The spirit has been made from sugar, and the person who used the still knew how to get the maximum amount of spirit at the ' least possible cost of time and money. The illicit still is, in short, an excel- lent apparatus. Even the spent "wash "—the solution that is thrown off after the spirit has been made—received the attention of the man who worl:ed the still, for this waste was made to run down a drain inside the stable itself; and so no smell of spirit could possibly get wafted out to the stv-ht- •

div.head: CLIFFORD'S INN IN JEOPARDY.
div.p: CLIFFORD'S INN IN JEOPARDY.

It looks as though one of the chief remain- ing landmarks of old London was doomed to pass away. After reference to the 'courts, Clifford's Inn is for sale. A moyement, how- ever, is mooted to preserve it intact, not only for its own sake and associations, but owing to its proximity to the Record Office, which contains many priceless • documents. To re place it by modern buildings would, it is argued, jeopardise the new public office by fire, and would obstruct its light, which is an important consideration. Clifford's Inn is the last of the old Inns of Chancery; and, like Gray's Inn, Lincoln's Inn, and Furnival's Inn, it grew up under the wgis of some great noble- man. In 1300 King Edward 11. granted to Robert de Clifford a messuage next to the

div.head: OLD CLIFFORD'S INN, WHICH IS TO BE SOLD.
div.p: OLD CLIFFORD'S INN, WHICH IS TO BE SOLD.

Church of St. Dunstan-in-the-West, and in 1344 he rented it to the students of law for ten pounds a year, This grant and lease arc the earliest of many quaint and interesting documents grouped round this historic old Spot. In ;1767 the hall was rebuilt, but the old wall is distinctly visible at the east end, which contains a fourteenth - century arch. The Clifford arms are over the Fleet Street entrance. The .hall has of late been used as the irt Workers' Guild, since it gradually dropped into disuse after the dinners had fallen to two a term. Prior to 1884, for many years the Society of Clifford's Inn was com- posed of five-and-twenty members; but since 1877 no new members have been admitted,
I • and the number has gradually dwindled. The Inn and its buildings are full of historic and antiquarian interest, and it will be a great pity if they cannot be preserved to London.
THE ANSON'S GUNS.

Recent discoveries recall a naval trageay of nearly a century ago. On December 27th, 1807, the frigate Anson foundered in Mounts Bay, and her commander, Captain Charles Lydiard, went to the bottom with a hundred of his crew. Since then the wreck has remained undisturbed and unlocated until recently, when Captain Anderson, of the West of England Salvage Company, discovered signs of wreckage upon the eastern shore of the bay. As these did not appear to be modern, but the remains of an old man-of- war, he reported the matter to the Admiralty. After sonic negotiations the Admiralty Board consented to sell the wreck to the Company, and since tIL they have lost no time in
HOW ONE OF THE GUNS LOOKED AFTER NEARLY 100 YE-kll*' SUBMERSION. •

proceeding with their ,search under the per- sonal superintendence of Captain Anderson. He himself located the wreck and made a descent from the Greencastle to the hulk of the Anson. At the time of her loss the man- of-war had forty-four guns on board, of which Captain Anderson has seen fifteen. Under one of these 6. chain was passed with no small difficulty, and it was safely hoisted up on board the Greencastle. It was found to be thickly encrusted with shingle, and several shots were attached to it. This old weapon is ten and a half feet long and has a 6-inch bore. It is expected that many of the other guns will be recovered, in addition to an im- portant collection of most interesting old plics_of the Navy of a century agoi

RAWCLIFFE CHARITY CUP. EARLESTOWN V. ST. HELENS TOWN

At Earlestown on Saturday in lovely weather. The homesters were very indifferently represented owing to the necessity of playing two teams in the field that day, one eleven operating at Chorleyoin the Charity Cup Competitien. No less than five new players were intro- duced into the team, these ,including a goalkeepernamed Pennington, brother of the Notts County custodian; Mox, one of the Bolton Wanderers; and Leach,a brother of the Earlestown player. The Town won the toss, and took advantage of the wind andhill,Bartley starting be- fore NO spectators. A clearance by Pennington put Leach in possession,and the inside left capped a magnificent run with a shot which defeated the custodian all to pieces. Immediately afterwards a pass from Ramsell enabled Howarth to put the own on equality again. Ten minutes before the interval Houghton placed the homesters ahead, whilst Dagnall again made the scores level a moment later. Howarth gave the Town the lead a few minutes before the whistle blew. Interval: St. Helens Town3,Earlestown 2. Final: Earlestown 4, St. Helens 3.
Primrose Day.

Sunday was the anniversary of the death, of Lord Beaconsfield and the rate earl's favourite flower was worn as a button-sole by many Warrington people. A very beautiful wreath of prnuruses was displayed on the balcony at the Conservative Club. Chasing a " Scorching " 'Bus. _ _ - •

Thom-as Hardy, one of the Motor Carriage Com- pany's drivers, recently took a 'bus load of lunatics from Prestwich to Winwick, and, on the return journey, careered through Patricroft w.th the 'bus and three h .rses at an alarming rate. He was charged at Eccles, on Monday, with furious driving, and fined 20s. and costs, his defence being that he had lost con- trol of the horses.—William Tonge, a Salford Cor- poration tramdriver, chased the 'bus, boarded it, and brought the horses to a standstill. In his opinion the horses were not beyond control.— Albert Bethel, manu- facturer, corroborated.

Elvin.Dowling, whilst in the Worcester cells, charged with drunkenness, made three determined but unsuccess- ful attempts at suicide by hanging—first with a rope she made out of a piece of cloth, then with a piece of string, and finally with a plait manufactured from her own hair. .

div.head: LATE MR. W. H„ ROBINSON.
div.p: THE LATE MR. W. H„ ROBINSON.
Funeral at Warrington Cemetery.
Total 79 Total for 7wkts 108

There was a large assembly of townspeople at the Warrington Cemetery on Saturday afternoon to witness the funeral of the late Mr. W. H. Robinson, 49, Wilson Patten-street, whose death was recorded in our last issue. The deceased gentleman was held in great respect by a large circle of friends and profound regret has been occasioned by his demise. He was a prominent Freemason and many members of the craft attended the obsequies. The last rites were conducted by the Rev. T. Bridge, Vicar of Poynton, near Macclesfield, an old friend of the deceased gentleman, and H. V. Pigot, Vicar of St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath (W.M. of the Lodge of Lights of Freemasons) and E. C. E. Carleton, Vicar of Holy Trinity Church. The chief mourners were: Mr. Arthur Robinson (Winnington), Mr. W. H. Robinson, and Mr. Leonard .Robinson (sons), Mr. Walter Greenhouse (son-in-law), Mr. Charles Heyes (nephew), of Southport; Mr. Henry Evans (Warrington) and Mr. John Henry (Chester). There were also pie- sent: Alderman Hutchinson' Dr. Joseph (deceased's medical adviser), Mr. Robert Henshall, Mr. Charles White, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, Mr. E. Birtles, Mr. Houghton, Mr. T. Tunstall, Mr. W. S. Howard, Mr. E. Richardson Mr. Jeffrey, Air. H. Hatton, Mr. G. Pilling, Mr. T. D. Amos, Councillor Bennett, Mr. G. Lomas, Mr. Joseph Potter and others. The Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club, of which deceased was the treasurer from its fortnation,vms represented by Mr. Reginald Silcock and Mr. Richard T. Fairclough (viqe-presidents), Mr. C. H. Unsworth (secretary), Mr. Thoinas Cooper (secre- tary of the bowling department), and Mr. J. W. Bibby (ceptain of the cricket team.) All the Freemasons pre- sent wore white ties and white gloves, and a sprig of acacia. The Lodge of Lights, 148, was represented by Bros. Thomas Grime' P.W., P.P.G.S.Dt F. G. Bennett, John Cowdell, Fred Howard, I.P.M.:s; R.. Shacklady, P.M., P,P.G.D.D:C. ; Arthur J. Willett, Rev. H. V. Pigot, W.M. ; John Rogerson, P.M. treasurer; W. Griffiths,Charles E. Bennett, T. J. Lee, Charles Leigh, S.D. ; A. G. Jones' C. ,Plunkett. J. H. Day, J.W. ; J. E. Warren, W. Waring, J. Hallwood, I.G. •, Charles J. Smith, NV. B. Roberts, P.M, P.P.G.D. ; H. F. Greenough, P.M. • Ashton Hayes, Charles W. Phillips, P.M., 758, P.P.G.A.D. of C. Ches. ; J. A. McGregor, S.W., 148; and John Sampson. Bro.. Hindley, P.M., was unable to attend. Those present from 1250, Sir Gilbert Greenall Lodge, were Bros. W. H. J. Jenkins, P.M. P.P.G.R. ; W. Rogers, W. Atherton, W. Coppock, H Shackleton, E. Rose, P.M., P.P.D.G., D.C., Thomas Atherton, Thomas G. Warhurst, C. G. McDowell, S.D.; William Whittaker, I.P.M. ; Alfred Jolley, G.D.; Southerden, T. 3. Hulse,S. G. Charity Lodge, 2,651, was represented by Bros. John Hesketh, P.M. 148, P.M. 2651; W. H. Woodcock, J.W. ; D. Tinnion, S.D.; and R. H. Pearson, P.M., P.P.G.D.' Bro. G. C. Taylor wrote apologizing for his non- attendance.

At the conclusion of the service at the graveside the Freemasons threw their sprigs of acacia on to the oak coffin. A very large number of floral tributes had been forwarded. including those from the Cricket and Bowling Club, Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., the Lodge of Lights, and the Charity Lodge of Freemasons. Bro. H. F. Greenough had charge of the arrangements and supplied the carriages.

The Examiner, Friday, April 24, 1903.

BROUGHTON RANGERS v. RUNCORN. '. This match, which was postponed on account of the semi-final tie between Oldham and Salford, was played on the Rangers' ground on Wednesday. The attendance was a poor one, as the result had no bearing on the championship,and little interest was taken in the match. From the kick-off the Rangers took up an attacking position, but Moran got his side out of difficulties by a splendid run, which was brought to a close by a fine tackle by Fielding. The Rangers still held the upper hand, mid after Wilson had failed to just get over the line,the ball came out to Shaw, who scoredatryfor the Rangers, which Wilson improved. At half-time the score was five points to nothing in favour of the home team. In lie second half Runcorn tried hard to get on level terms, but they found the defence of the home backs too strong for them, and the end of a well-fought game was—Broughton Rangers, one goal and one try (five points) ; Runcorn nothing.

WAR,RINGTON V. BR ADFORD.

Warrington journeyed to Bradford on Saturday to play their last away match, and if possible, to avenge the defeat sustained at Wilderspool. The team was representative, with the one important excep- tion that Isherwood, the captain, was an absentee, Brookes from the "A" team filling the vacancy at centre. There was only a small crowd of about 1,500 spectators. The teams and officials-were:—

Bradford—Boyes, back; Sinton, Mosby, Heseltine,and Dunbavin, three-quarter backs; Mandes and Brear, half backs; Broadley (captain), B. Smales, Turner, Carroll, Lewis, Sharratt, Laidlaw, and Dunn, forwards. Warrington—Hallam, back; Fish, Brookes, Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs; Edmunds and Duck- worth, half hacks; W. Swift, Hai. -ner, Edmondson, Forster, Coleman, Naylor, Swift, and Jolley, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes. Touch judges, Mr. J. Henry, jun., Holbeck, and Mr. G. Holdsworth,Halifax. ' Bradford lost the toss,and Broadley kicked off against a moderate wind, at once attacking. A nice opening was made by Marsden, from which Sinton scored a try. Mosby's goal-kick was t failure. Harris, for Warring- ton, pat in a fine run from-his own quarters, and kicked the ball over Boyes' head, but only a minor resulted. With the game at the centre Sinton broke his collar- bone, and Bradford had to play to the end with 14 men. Warrington thus aided attacked, Harris scoring easily, Fish kicking the goal. Just before half-time Fish scored another try, and Bradford were five points in arrears at the change of ends.—On the resumption, the home team played up well, and Laidlaw, after a lot of passing, scored, Boyes failing at goal. A few minutes later the latter player made amends by kicking a penalty goal, thus equalising. Dunbavin, by fast following up, put this side three points ahead by scoring an unim- proved try, but just before the call of time Dicken son added a try, which Fish did not improve upon, and the game ended in a draw. Result :—Bradford 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points), Warrington 1 goal and 3 tries (11 points.)

div.head: HUNSLET v. RUNCORN
div.p: HUNSLET v. RUNCORN

This return match was played at Parkside, before a moderate gate. Runcorn *on the toss, and A. Gold- thorpe kicked off against the wind. After one or two scrummages near the centre Richardson and Price got away to the home line with a splendid dribble, which ended in the latter scoring. Farmer failed at goal. Hunslet had a spell of attacking, and Albert Goldthorpe just missed dropping a goal. However, another score for Runcorn was soon forthcoming. Jolley getting possession from a scrummage passed to Richardson, who after a long run, transferred to Butterworth, who scored a fine try. Farmer again failed to add the extra points, Near the interval Hunslet pressed, but could not score. With the wind in the second half Hunslet attacked, and the visiting full back touched down. From a wide pass by Everson, A. G oldthor•pe dropped a fine goal, which was directly followed by a penalty from the same player. Runcorn then started around of pass ng,which ended in Moran scoring a try, Farmer failing at goal. Just on time A. Goldthorpe dropped another goal, and the game ended with the score :—Runcorn 3 tries (9 points), Hunslet 3 goals (6 points). Teams : Hunslet—H. Place, back; Bewley, W. Goldthorpe, Brimskill, and J. Whiteley, three-quarter backs; A. Everson, and A. E. Goldthorpe, half backs; T. Walsh, H. Wilcox, W. Brooke, W. Wray, J. Shooter, O'Brien, Fothergill, and J. Ramage, forwards. Runcorn—Harrison, back; Jottes, Butterworth,Price, and Moran, three-quarter backs; Jolley and Richardson, half backs; Walker, Farmer, Moulton, Woods, Reece, W. Houghton, Dixon, and Messenger, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford. Touchjudges,Mr. F. Bennett, Batley, and-Mr. G. Wilson, Manningham.

div.head: WIDNES v. BRIGEIOUSE RANGERS,
div.p: WIDNES v. BRIGEIOUSE RANGERS,

Played at Widnes, before 2,000 spectators. The Rangers had, only 14 men. The visitors won the toss, and for a time the game was confined to the centre. Then Widnes got into their opponents' quarters, but just before the interval Tilley thulled badly, and Baker following well up,scored near the posts. Saville added two more points by kicking a goal. Half-time score: --Brighouse Rangers, 1 goal 1 try (5 points) ; Widnes, nil.—On resuming,Widnes attacked strongly, and a num- ber of scrummages took place on the Rangers' line. When the play was at the centre Alf. Taylor received a pass, and after a tricky run, he scored at the corner.. Tilley failed at goal. Widnes kent up the attack, and Lally dropped a goal, but the ball touched one of the Brighouse men. Just before the close Tilley placed a penalty goal. Result :—Widnes, 1 goal 1 try (5 points). Teams : B ighouse Rangers.—Hartley, back; Walker' Sutcliffe, Saville and Baker, three-quarter backs; Ross and Mullarkey, half backs; Kilburn, Armitage, Banks, Ho lroyd, Miller, Ridgdale, and Wolfenden, forwards. Widnes.—Tilley, back • Pecock, Rispan, I. Taylor and Lally, half backs ; ispey, Cockram, Riley, Webster, Lynch, Leyshon, Power, and McDonald, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Oakland, Wakefield. Touch judges, Messrs. A. Lees, Leigh, and J. Graham, St. Helens.

div.head: WIGAN v ST. HELENS
div.p: WIGAN v ST. HELENS

These teams met at Wigan, before 5,000 spectators. St. Helens had the treeze in the initial half, and as a result of a faulty kick by Mason, Jones registered a try, the visitors leading by 3 points to nil at the interval.

In the second half, as the outcome of smart work by Anderson, Green was afforded a capital chance, and ho opened Wigan's account with a try. St. Helens added a goal, kicked by Hall, and the result was :—St. Helens 1 goal and 1 try (5 points), Wigan 1 try (3 points). Teams :

Wigan—Mason, back: Barr, Green, A. Duffy, and Rouse, three-quarter ba6s ; Anderson and Glea,ve, half- backs; Ball, Collier, .Robinson, Barton,Ellison,/Beesley, Hatton and H. Duffy, forwards. St. 11,--lens—Foulkes, back; Porter, Liversage, W. Briers, and Jones, three-quarter backs; Hall and. Pennington, half-backs; Lee, Mawson, Thompson, Green; T. Briers, Mooney,Mercer,and Whiteley,forwards.
RefE;ree, Mr.' W. -McCutcheon, Oldha. Touch judges, Messrs. W. J. Britton, Leigh, and A. Critchley, Widnes.
HULL v. LEIGH.

Played on the Hull Boulevard Ground, bofora a small atteleflanse. Leigh won the toss, and Hull started so well that it was marvellous how,the visitors so long survived the attack. Play had been in 'progress some time, however, before MOXOI.I ran over unopposed from a pass by Cook, and Parkinson added the goal. Before half-time,,liirk got posse,sSion, and gave to Boardman, who scored Under tlO cross-bar, and Molyneux had no trouble in equalising. The second half was uninterest- ing. Hull 'did niost of the attacking, and Parry in his tenacious minner worked his way through, and got over, giving the home team an uaconverted try. The game resulted :—Hull 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points), Leigh 1 goal, .1 try (5 points).

div.head: HUDDERSFIELD v. SWINTON.
div.p: HUDDERSFIELD v. SWINTON.
This return match was played at Fartown, betor 4,00 spectators. Swinton 1, goal 1 try •(5 points), Huddersfield nil.
BATLEY v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS
This match was played on the Mount Pleasant ground, in the presence of a fair number of spectators. Result: Batley 2 goals and 1 try (7 paints), Hull 11;ingston Hovers 1 goal and 1 try (5 points).

div.head: HALIFAX v. OLDHAM.
div.p: HALIFAX v. OLDHAM.

Played at Halifax before 10,000 spectators. Little kicked off for Halifax, and play was even. At half- time neither side had scored. The game during the first few minutes of the second half was also well contested. Each side pressed in turn, and then Rigg enabled Hali- fax to attack. The ball eventually went to Joe Riley, who promptly dropped a goal. R,igg- soon afterwards scored behind the uprights; Hadwen kicking 4 goal from the place. Wedgewood also• crossed the line, but this time Hadwen failed at goal. Civil and S.pottiswoode, two Oldham players,retired just before the finish. The visitors although short-handed, made a final effort to score, Topham being held just outside, after a clever bout of passing. Result :—Halifax 2 goals, 2 tries (10 points), Oldham nil.

div.head: HULL V. SALFORD.
div.p: HULL V. SALFORD.

Hull prwed themselves too strong for Salford on Monday by defeating them by a margin of seven points. From the kick-off Hull began to attack strongly, but some finedefensive play by *Smith kept them at bay for ashort Mtn?. Eventually Fulton broke through the Salfctrd defence and scored a try, which Parkinson im- proved. Hull continued to attack, and another try was scored by Sowerby, which Parkinson again im- proved,* Whilst before half-time Parkinson placed a penalty goal. When ends were changed Hull had the large lead of twelve points to nothing. Salfbrd played up strougly in the second half, but for a long time the home defence prevailed and, it was not until the clos- ing stages of the game that the Hull defence was pene- trated. This was done by Norris, who scored a try after a round of passing between the backs, and Lomas placed a goal. Nothing further was scored, and the game ended :—Hull, three goals and two tries (twelve points) ; Salford, one goal and try (five points.)

div.p: WIGAN v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.
This match was played at Wigan ou Wednesday. The game eventually ended in a win for Wigan by three goals (six points), to Hull Kingston lovers one goal two (points).

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

THE WARRINGTON CUP. THELW ALL VICTORIOUS IN THE FINAL T. Great interest centred in the final tie for the War- rington Cup which was decided on the ground of Rich- monds' Athletic Club, Padgate-lane, on Saturday after- noon. Thelwall and Oughtrington Park were the op- posing teams And in anticipation of a keen contest about 3,000 spectators assembled. The game was splendidly fought from beginning to end, but Thelwall had the good fortune to gain the advantage in the second half and came (Mt victorious by two goals to one. At the outset, Thelwall faced the wind, Woods setting the ball in motion. Oughtrington were the first to attack, and in the first minute,Thelwall were forced to concede a corner. Reynolds, however, averted the danger. Leah ,was prominent with a tricky run, and passing across to A. Lord, the outside man put in a good centre, but Kite came to the rescue, and danger was thus averted. Reynolds and Howard took play to the other end, but the attack was only brief, for after Thompson had kicked clear, Leah received the ball, and after out- manceuvring the backs, sent in a hot shot which brought Smith to his knees. However, he cleared at the ex- pense of a corner. This was well placed, but Thompson kicked high over the cross-bar. Combined play between Guest, Woods, Price, and Riley forced the game to-the Oughtrington end, but Thompson and Woods cleared, and the right wing once more took up the running, another corner being forced with- out result. The Parkites continued to monopolise the play, but the shooting was4oo feeble to gain anything tangible. Thelwall then put in some fine forcing tactics and made matters lively for the Park defenders. The game As stopped for a few moments owing to an injury to Woods. Oughtrington again put on pressure and from a shot by Lord, Smith again distinguished himself and it was mainly due to his cleverness that Oughtring- ton failed to score. Thelwall transferred operations to the other end and C. Woods shot in, but Smith was safe and sure. Thelwall again made several onslaughts on the Park goal, but met with a ,stubborn defence. Half time arrived with no score. On resuming, Thelwall at once got down in brilliant fashion, and Smith was forced to handle in the first minute. An exciting tussle next followed near the goal mouth, and the Oughtring- ton backs had all their work cut out to keep them at bay. Relief came from a free kick, and though the Park men strove hard, they could make no headway against their opponents, who showed a magnificent defence. Thelwall advanced by neat combination, and Thompson, mis- kicking, let in Guest, who shot in hard, but Smith fisted out. Riley,however, met the rebound and scored ami@l loud cheering. Oughtrington had rather the best of matters after this and the Thelwall, goal had one or two narrow escapes. this, leaders again threatened Smith's charge in vigorous style, and a stinging shot from'Rey- noldsalmost ended in a score. The goalkeeper saved at the expense of a corner. Howard placed well in, the sphere eventually going to Riley, who made no mistake and scored the second goal.- A series of attacks by Oughtrington next followed, and it was marvellous how the Thelwall goal escaped being captured. Play slowed down so uewhat after this, neither side shewine,c, to great advantage. A breakaway by the Thelwall forwards came to nothing, Leah being the saviour of his side. In the last minute of the match, the Oughtring- ton men gained a corner, and this being well placed, the ball was rushed through. Thelwall thus won a splendid game by two goals to one. After the match, the cup SEQUEL TO and medals were presented by Mr. Fulton Smith. The supporters of the Thelwall team were naturally very jubilant at the result, and as the club drove home the cup was proudly exhibited, and cheers were repeatedly raised.

div.p: -WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Annual Meeting. Election of Chairman.

There was a full attendance at the annual meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday. The Clerk (Mr. J. O. Sutton) presided over the proceedings during the election of Chairman. There were present: Mrs. Clay, the Rev. Father Wilson, Dr. Patterson, Dr. Murray, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, G. Pilling, J. Billings, J. Backhouse, T. H. Ashcroft, S. Davies, J. Paytoi,4l. Clarke, R. Forshaw, J. Robinson, T. Halton, William Houghton, J. W. Knowles, J. Ball, T. Turton, G. Mather and T, Ritchie. The officials present were: Mr. J. C. Sutton (olerk),Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk) Mr. F. Gate tworkhouse master), and Mr. A. Wright (superintendont of Padgate Schools). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.
THF. tLERK'S SIXTIETH YEA.R OF OFFICIAL LIFE.

CLERK stated at the outset that the present year was the third and last year of office of the members. The Board would eN.pire at the conclusion of the term of office of the present chairman. The present was the 35th year in succession he had been appointed to the chair, permanently for a few years and temporarily for 31 years. He had also entered uponhis 60th year of official life. Daring that time they had lost many friends,and he thought that Mr. Charles White was the only sur- vivor of his colleagues at the time of his first connec- tion with the Guardians. They had lost many friends from time to time, and the most recent disease was that of his old friend Mr. Robert Garnett. He sat on the same form at school with him. He was a most useful, intelligent and active guardian for some years. How long, the Clerk continued, he (Mr. Sutton) might remain in his official position was a matter of uncertainty. The work of the Board as well as of the Runt! District Council was growing, and he was not sure that it would not be of a more responsible character than he cared for. The first business was the appointment of chairman. Dr. PATTERSON proposed Mr. Brooks for the position. They knew, he said, how zealous he had been in the dis- charge of his duties as a member of the Board. He thought Mr. Brooks could be well trusted to act as chairman. (Hear, hear.) Mr. KNowLEs, in seconding the proposition, said that in Mr. Brooks they would find an able and excellent chairman. One thing he particularly noticed abouthim and that was his broadmindedness. They found some people who were naturally born with fads and peculiari- ties, but they did not find any of them in Mr. Brooks. He would be an ideal chairman. Mr. S. DAVIES said he believed that inappointing Mr. Brooks they would be appointing one who would do his duty faithfully. He had had great experience and he had carried outthe work of the House Committee to the entire satisfaction of the members. He was not a man of many words, but he was a thorough worker, aud was never tired of doing what he could for the benefit of the institution. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON supported the proposition. Mr. G. PILLING said he had seen more of .I‘fr. Brooks work than his seconder by a great deal. (Laughter.) He felt certain, they would have in Mr. Brooks a worthy occupant of the position. Mr. R. FORSHA NV also supported the proposition which was carried unanimously. The CLERK said he had pleasure in inviting Mr. Brooks to take the chair. At the same time he might say on lehalf of the officials that they most cordially concurred with the appointment made by the Board. Mr. BROOKS had a hearty reception on taking the chair. He said he wished to thank the members for electing him to that office. He knew he was following in the footsteps of many men whom it was an honour to follow. It was a position which any member of the Board ought to be proud to fill and he was gratified at being elected. He thanked the members for the kindly feelings which had been expressed and for the generous confidence which their vote implied. It remained for him to do his best and to justify that confidence (Applause.)

div.head: V ICE-CHAIRAiAN.
div.p: V ICE-CHAIRAiAN.

The CLERK pointed out that it had been usual to appoint a senior and a junior vice-chairman. The Local Government Board had now decided that it was not necessary to appoint a junior vice-chairman. Mr. JOSHUA. BALL moved the appointment of Mr. J. W. Knowles for the position of vice-chairman. Mr. Knowles, he pointed out,had held the position of junior vice-chairman for two or three years. Mr:WILMA:It HOUGHTON seconded and Mr. Mather and Dr. Patterson supported. The proposition was unanimously carried. Mr. KNOWLES thanked the members for the appoint- ment. Whilst in the position of junior vice-chairman he had had nothing to do. He must admit that he had not attended to his duties as he should have liked, but still when there was anything important on hand he was generally in his place. The resolution was carried. The Asylum Visitation Committee was revised to admit of the partial re-appointment of Guardians not lately serving thereon. THE VALUER 'S SALARY. On the proposition of Mr. G. PILLING, it was deci- ded that Mr. William Owen be re-appointed to assist the Assessment Committee in the valuation of the several hereditaments (rateable) in the Union for the further period of one year at a salary or remuneration of £2OO for such year, such remuneration to cover and includa all travelling and other expenses out of pocket.

div.head: CO MAE ITT EES .
div.p: THE CO MAE ITT EES .

Mr. PILLING moved "That except as to any change that may be resolved upon the present acting members of the respective committees and representatives of the Board be re-appointed and re-elected for the ensuing year and with the same anthorityand powers as hitherto exercised—that all guardians present at meetings for administration of relief be entitled to take part in the proceedings, and that the members of the Ladies' Visit- ing Committee visit the House, the Infirmary and the Padgate Schools at discretion." Mr. ASHCROFT thought it would be advisable to have a list prepared of attendances at the committee meetings. The,CLEEtii. said so far as the Assessment Committee was concerned he could state that there was most regular attendance given at the meetings.
THE EXTENSIONS AT THE WORKHOUSE. ACCEPTANCE OF TENDERS. _

Mr. Owirs Produced the tenders which he had re- ceivAd from builders for the proposed extensions at the Workhouse. The Chairman opened the tenders andsaid they were as follows :—For extensions to wash-houses, Joseph Dolan, £1,772; H. Fairclough, £1,840; R. W. Collin, £1920; C. NV. Davenport, £1,984. For exten- sions for vagrants' use, Joseph Dolan, £560; H. Fair- dough 609; R. NV.- Collin, £557; C. NV. Davenport, £606 12s. 6d. Mr. PILLIN. G moved that the tenders of Mr. Joseph • Dolan for both works be accepted. ▪ Mr.-A. J. JOLLEY seconded and this was agreed to. The CLERK intimated that the Local Government Board had issued an order authorising a loan of £2,225 for the extensions mentioned, the loan to be repaid with interest within a period not exceeding 25 years.

div.head: PA D.S.TE SCHOOLS.
div.p: PA D.S.TE SCHOOLS.
Mr. MOZELY, Local Government Board Inspector of Poor Lavs Schools, reported on his recent examination of the children, which was of a satisfactory character.
13011 SE COMMITTEE

This committee recommended that Nurse Irwin of the Meek Workhouse, be appointed nurse at a salary of £27 10s., with the usual allowances. The committee intim- ated that they had passed votes of thanks to the chair- man, vice-chairman, master and matron, and the staff generally for their services during the year. In the annual report of the Ladies Committee, which was sub- mitted to the House Committee, reference was made to the marked improvement in the discipline of the inmates. On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr MATHER, the minutes of the Committeewere approved.

div.head: 'THE OVERSEERS_ OF GREA.T _SAN-KEY.
div.p: 'THE OVERSEERS_ OF GREA.T _SAN-KEY.

The CLERK stated that he had received a letter from Mr. Smith, the assistant overseer for Great Sankey, informing him that the appointment of overseers had Uot been made, as the Parish Council was Unable to form a quorum. The Clerk informed the Board that that day was the last on which the appointments could be made. The power rested with the Guardians to re-appoint the overseers, if the Parish Council failed to do so. The last overseers were Messrs. ThomasHalton, George Thompson, and Joseph Wright. He was told Mr. Wright had left the district. Mr. HA LTON said if he was in order he would move the appointment of Mr. George Thompson and himself as overseers. Mr. WILLIAM HOUGHTON seconded, and the proposi- tion was carried. This was all the business.

Death of Mr. T. Broome, of Croft. The death occurred suddenly on Saturday evening of Mr. Thomas Broome, Littletown, Croft. Deceased, who had attained his seventy-fifth year, had been, a resideut in the parish for about 45 years, and was widely known and respected. Although for some time in failing health he was able to move freely about until stricken down, death being attributed to failure of the heart's action.

div.head: SEAWEED AS A MEDICINE.
div.p: SEAWEED AS A MEDICINE.
ITS MARVELLOUS EFFECT UPON THE

A meeting of the representatives of the local friendly societies, convened by the Town Clerk, for the purpose of appointing a representative on the new Education Committee was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall on Monday. The press were not admitted. Mr. Haley presided. The following societies were represented :—Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, 7 re- presentatives; Foresters, 5 • Independent Order of Druids, 5; Ancient Order of Rechabities, 4; Gardeners' Society, 2; Grand United Order of Oddfellows, 2; and Ancient Order of Shepherds, 4; or a total of 31,. The Chairman alluded to the present position of affairs and explained how it was that the Friendly Societies' Council appointed a representative without consulting the friendly societies generally, but exception was taken to the statement, being of a somewhat lively character. It was proposed that the voting should be taken by ballot, but the motion was dgfeated.—Mr. Llewellyn Davies, of the Foresters' Society, proposed the election of Mr. William Bibby, the nominee of the Friendly Societies' Council, and a member of the Druids' Society, and this was seconded by Mr. William Wright,•of .the Ancient Order of Rechabites—Mr. Ellis R. Clare,the Provincial Grand Master of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows,submitted the name of Mr. Thomas S. Steel, and this was seconded by Mr. F. J. Emson, of the same societv.—Mr. Lawrence Weir of the Ancient Order of hepherds, proposed the appointment of Mr. Peter Edgar, the District Secretary of the Shepherds' Society. This was seconded by Mr, Miller of the same society. It was decided "that the successful Candidate should have a clear majority." The voting resulted as follows:—For Mr. Bibby 14; for Mr. Steel, 11 ; for Mr. Edgar 2. A second vote vas then taken, Mr. Edgar's name being omitted, and the result was found to be as follows :—For Mr. Bibby, 14; for Mr. Steel; 12. Mr. Bibby was, therefore,elected. It will be seen that although there were 31 delegates present, on the first voting only 27 votes were recorded, and 26 on the second voting. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Haley for presiding, to Mr. R. E. Pooley (hon. secretary of the Friendly Societies' Council), and to the Mayor for the nse of the Council Chamber.

div.head: AT WORK.
div.p: AT WORK.
THE APPOINTMENT OF MANAGERS.
The Examiner, Friday, April 24, 1903. WARRINGTON PROPERTY OWNERS AND RATES.

Mr. J. P. JONES: Every five years. The last revision was on the Ist February, 1901. Mr. R. .LEIGII ; Most of my assessments were raised. Mr. STEPHEN DALE: A lot of mine were raised. I have not heard of any being lowered. (Laughter.) . _

Mr. J. P. JONES saill there were a nuniber Of property owners who had told him theriwould not be able to be present at that meeting, but they were in sympathy with its objects and would assist it in evety way possible. In answer to a question by the SECRETARY, Mr. JONES said the assessment of a cottage rented at 4s. 3d. a week was the same as that for one rented At 4s. 6d. a week. Both came under the same basis of assessment.

Mr. HENSHALL : What is the highest assessment you can compound at? Mr. ENGLAND: £l3 gross. Mr. HENSIIALL then moved' that a committee be formed to frame rules and also to advise as to the best way in which property could be raised. He believed he was right in assuming that they were all anxious to raise the rents.

The CHAIRmAN:We shall have to raise the property or get the assessments reduced. Mr. FLEMING : I don't think you will get the assess- ments reduced. Mr. HENSHALL : That is not the line of least resist- ance.

Mr.J. P. JONES: Where there is a combined effort you don't know what you can do. I don't know when there was a feeling so strong among , the property owners as at the present time. OUGHT THE CORPORATION TO COLLECT THE
RATES?
Mr. HARRISON: I think the Corporation ought to collect the rates.
The CHAIRMAN: The question arises whether the Corporation would be compelled to collect the rates if we refused to do so.

Mr. HENSHALL said it might raise a point in law. He supposed the landlords were not responsible for the rates. It was a commercial agreement between the Corporation and the property owners, by which theland- lord of property guaranteed the Corporation immunity from loss and inconvenience and expense of collection, and the Corporation on their part allowed him a dis- count. If the landlord found it was not to his interest to collect the rates he could terminate the agreement. Mr. DALE: That is the position. A DEPUTATION TO WAIT UPON THE CORPORATION.

Mr. ENGLAND thought the best plan would be for them to see how best they could work in harmony with the Corporation, and at the same time do the best they could for the tenants. , How that was to be arrived at was somewhat difficult of solution. There were at least two ways in which it could be solved. He did not think for a moment that they would be able to get the assess- ments reduced. That, he thought, they would all feel from past experience would be labour wasted. (Hear, hear.) But he thought they ought to be able to get composition allowed on higher rates of assessment. If they were allowed a composition on houses assessed at £l6 instead of £l3 it would be a concession to the property owners. The matter would require carefully working out and it would probably be a matter 'for the Borough treasurer. There was also another way which had been adopted in some places. He understood that under the Act of 1867 the Poor Rate was collected from each tenant individually. It seemed to him that if this education rate could be collected from each tenant by the Corporation it might prove a blessing in disguise because it would have the effect of making every householder and ratepayer take more interest in Parliamentary and municipal work. The property owners did not want to get more than the rate and the tenants on the other hand didnot want to pay more than the rate. The education rate was not like an ordinary rate for street improvement or lighting pur- poses, for education was a matter which touched every householder. He did not think householders wanted to get out of paying fer edudation as he was of opinion that they were quite prepared to do the proper thing. He would suggest that a deputation wait upon the Cor- poration and ask them to mutually consider along, with the property owners the best way of arriving at'a solu- tion as regarded thequestion of rate collecting. The CHAIRMAN said it would be advisable to first appoint a sub-committee to draft a code of rules to be presented at a subsequeot meeting. Mr. HENSHALL moved that such a sub-committee be appointed. .

a kr. DALE seconded and it was agreed to. It was decided that the following should form the sub-committee: Messrs. E. England, R. Henshall,,L. Fleming, S. Dale, and R. Leigh, with the officers as ex-officio members.

div.head: AN ASSOCIATION AT WORK.
div.p: AN ASSOCIATION AT WORK.
Deputation to wait upon the Corporation.

The startling increase in the rates of Warrington has, caused the property owners to form an association oI their own for the protection of their interests. The initial steps were taken at a preliminary meeting held a fortnight ago and on Thursday last week an- other meet was held at Raddon Court, Latch- ford. Raddon Court has been recently ac- quired by a private company and the palatial residence of the late Captain Reynolds is now being used for the purposes of a club, in connection with which a tennis club has been recently formed. It was in this building that a number of property owners assembled on Thursday evening under the auspices of the newly teemed Warrington and District Property Owners' Association. The chair was occupied by Mr. Joseph Mounfield. THE CHAIRMAN SPEAKS OF THE NEED OF AN

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

In the course of his introductory remarks the CHAIRMAN said he was waited upon by the secretary of the association (Mr. Lawton) and informed that at the last meeting it was proposed that he (Mr. Mounfield) should be asked if he would be the president of the Association. He was very much surprised to find that he was requested to take an important position of that kind. He did not know'whether he would be the right , man. in the right place, but he could say that the I Association had his sympathy. An association of that kind was absolutely necessary. (Hear, hear.) He was informed that it was to be thoroughly unpolitical in its objects. He could remember similar associations hav- ing been formed in Warrington and afterwards wrecked. Men took positions for a short time, and when their purposes were served and when their axes were ground, then the association was left to take care of itself. He hoped they would steer clear of any diffi- culties of that sort. In the first place they must • look to their interests as property owners, and look to them in a business-like manner. They did not' want either cranks or faddists, or men who wished to serve their own interests in spite of someone else. They wanted the business done on business lines and in a thoroughly straightforward manner. (Hear, hear.) If they did that he thought the association would hold together and they would all reap the benefit of it. Not only would they be benefited personally, but he believed the town its2,lf would be benefited by an association of that kin. (Hear, hear.) It wasa pity that the association was not formed a little sooner. He thought they ought to have, been represented on the Education Committee. (Hear hear.) The Education Committee would have thespend- nig of a great amount of money. He did not mean to suggest that they, should cripple education —(hear, hear)—but they ought to stop any extravagance. That Was why he thought they ought to have been represented on that committee. There was such a thin; as efficiency without extravagance and there wagon the other hand a cheeseparing policy which saved a penny and lost a pound. (Hear' hear.) They wanted to have at the head of all municipal affairs practical business men. He did not think he would be wrong when he said that thousands of pounds had been wasted through having men at the head of affairs who were not practical business men. That was a thing to be avoided if possible. Whilst he was not prepared to enter the Council himself, still he thought they ought to keep an eye on appointments of that kind and see to it that the men who were placed on the Council were men who had something at stake and who had business qualifications for the duties they were called to perform. That was his apology for being there. He did not look upon his appointment to the presidency of the association as a permanent one, but he took it pro tem and if someone better qualified to serve their purposes turned up, he would be prepared to stand down in his favour. He was prepared to do what he could to help forward the association. (Applause.) on THE PREVIOUS MEETING.

The SECRETARY (Mr. Lawton) read the minutes of the previous meeting at which it was decided to form an association. It was agreed to ask Mr. Mounfield to be president, Mr. Lawton was appointed secretary, and Mr. Gittens treasurer.
The minutes were passed. A COMMITTEE WANTED.

The CHAIRMAN suggested that the meeting should now take a step further and appoint a committee to form rules, register the society and obtain members. They cottld not expect people to come running to them in the first instance, but he thought the object of the _Associa- tion was one that would recommend itself to all pro- perty owners and ratepayers. (Hear, hear.)
FORMER RATEPAYERS'•ASSOCIATIONS A FIASCO.

Mr. STEPHEN DA.LE said the real objects of a rate- payers association were very manifold. The chief thing was to protect the interests of the ratepayers and be a power in the town. They had, had three associations formed in Warrington and as far as his knowledge went each one had been a fiasco. Theyhad not beensupported as they ought to have been, they were not worked on satisfactory lines, and not conducted in the same manner fis successful associations in other towns are conducted. His previous experience of other Rate- payers Associations in Warrington was that they were called upon to pay their money and support the associa- tion, but it had ended "in some sort of wind" and nothing had been done. (Laughter.) Previous associa- tions had been the laughing stock of "the powers that be "—those whom it had been intended to hold in check. (Hear, hear.) CAUSES OF PAST FAILURES TO BE AVOIDED.

Mr. ROBERT HENSHALL said he was not old enough to recapitulate the 'causes, of the failure of previous ratepayers' associations, but he was oldenough to know of their failures and the Chairman had already referred to some of the contributory causes. Men had joined previous associations, who, in the words of George Eliot, had " christened private grudges by the name of public zeal." They had axes to grind and personal animus to gratify andwhen that was done their interest in the association ceased. At the previous meeting the question of an increase of rents was discussed. It was felt that the anticipated increase in the rates of is. 2d. in the X would force the property owners from motives of self protection into some combined action and it was thought that would be the initial step in forming a strong property owners' association. It was recognised then that the past had bean strewn with wrecks and failures, but there were some of them young enough and foolish enough to hope that by the faults and failures of the past associations they might avoid those causes which had contributed to their decline and to theiralienation from the purposes for which they were formed. Their immediate object it was felt was two-fold. In the first place it was combined action in the raising of rents, and in the second place an attempt to induce the authorities to raise the basis on which compounding was allowed. At present the compound- ing of rates was not allowed on assessments of more than £l3 gross, and it was felt that the amount ought to be raiSed so as to allow a house let at Gs. a week to be included in the compoundage system. It was felt that these were two pressing and concrete things that would secure the practical sympathy and support of the whole of the property owners of the town. HIGH ASSESSMENTS AND SMALL WATER RATE 'ALLOWANCES.

Mr. WORTIIINGToN said he had been connected with several ratepayers associations but they all seemed to have come to nothing: Referring to the suggested in- crease of rents he pointed out that if ,the rent of a cottage was raised from 4s. to 4s. 3d. per week, the first thing. that would be done by the Assessment Com- mittee would be to raise the assessment. If they raised the rental of a 4s. house to 4s. 3d. the increase in the assessment would be 10s. and on that increased assess- ment rates amounting to 7s. 4d. in the 2 would have to be paid. It would therefore be seen that while the extra 3d. per week would bring in 12s. 6d. a year, the rat(' collector would want nearly ss. of it. Not only was it unpleasant to increase the rents but they ran greater risk .of not being able to collesct them in full. He was of opinion that the first thing the association should do was to get the assessments dropped. The assessments were fixed on a basis suggested by the late Mr. Tunstall and he (Mr. Worthington) was of opinion that the figure was too high for cottageproperty. If the property owners could Induce the Assessment Committee to make a small reduction in the assessment of cottage property then the owners would be in a better position. He felt that something Must be done in the way of raising rents to meet the additional rates,but under the present basis of assessment if they raised the rent 3d. per cottage, the results would be to the advantage oC the Corporation as the increased assessment would take the full benefit of such an increased rent. He suggested that a strong deputation of property owners should wait upon the Assessment Committee and ask the com- mittee to reduce the assessments on cottage property. There was another matter that attention should be called to and that was the composition allowed on the water rate. He thought there ought to be the samg composition allowed on the water rate as there was upon the poor rate and improvement rate, because owners of cottage property were obliged to pay the water rate if the cottages were empty. Cottages were constantly becoming empty and he did not see why the same com- position was not allowed on the water rate as upon the other rates. The property owner stood in exactly the same position with regard to the water rate, and the existing arrangement was an unfair one to the owner who was called upOn to pay the rate whether the houses were empty or not. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: ASSESSMENTS RAISED NOT REDUCED.
div.p: ASSESSMENTS RAISED NOT REDUCED.
The CHAIRMAN said he was of opinion that there would be some difficulty to get the assessments reduced in view of the present extraordinary expenditure in the town. '

Mr. J. PROCTOR JONES said he understood that th present assessments would not be inferfered with until the year 1906. If the property owner raised his rents now he would have the benek of that increased rent until the year 1906. Mr. ROBERT LEIGH: Are not the assessments re- vised every three years?

Mr. ENGLAND said the matter he had suggested ought to be taken in hand pretty quickly as it would take some time to formulate. ascheme if the Corporation fell in with the suggestion that had been made with refer- ence to raising the basis on which compoundage was allowed from .Cl 3 to £l6 and the collection of the edu- cation rate. He would move that a large and influential deputation of proporty owners waitupon the Corporation . _

. - The CHAIRIIIAI,i pointed out thai if the concession were granted with reference to raising the basis on which compoundage was allowed, it would not affect the bulk of property owners. Mr. ENGLAND: We could resolve upon a plan of action. Mr. DATA,: said such a concession as that alluded to would not be a general help to property owners. It would improve the position of men who owned property for which they charged ss. a week. Under existing cir- cumstances with reference to compoundage it paid an owner just as well to charge ss. as ss. 6d. The concession would also help the next class of property. that which was let at 6s. a lweek. It would therefore only help a few property owners. As an association they mnst go in for an all-round advantage. (Hear,hear.) He did not see how the association could do anything for the ratepayer who paid his own rates, perhaps o,n a house .£25 a year or more. The CHAIRMAN: We can benefit him by keeping down the expenditure of the town and preventing extravagance. Mr. ENGLAND: We need to arrange a plan of action.

_ Mr. J. P. JONES: There is no doubt we shall get on better with the Corporation by going as h deputation. It will do good. NO DESIRE TO BE HARSH WITH THE TENANTS. The CHAIRMAN said he was certain they were all in favour of working amicably with the Corporation and its officials and doing 'justice to the tenants They had no desire to be harsh or hard with he tenants. • (Hear, hear.) Their wishes were to keep rents as low as they could, but when they .were called upon .to such an extent as they were at the present time, they were bound to devise some means to meet it. What withthe heavy income-tax and the heavy Borough rates, something must be done. They had no wish whatever to fly in the face of the officials or give them trouble. They desired to work amicably with them and they hoped that spirit would be reciprocated. His exprience of the officials at the Town Hall led him to believe that they would do what they could for the property owners, and that if they approached them in a proper spirit that spirit would be reciprocated. (Hear, hear.) Let them try to come to some under- standing that would be reasonable and fair and right (Applause.) It was decided that the Secretary should place him- self in communication with the Corporation asking them to receive a deputation of property owners with refer- ence to the new rates. It was also agreed that the secretary should communicate with those present when a reply had been received from the Corporation so that they might form the deputation.

div.head: Hill Cliffe Baptist Chapel.
div.p: Hill Cliffe Baptist Chapel.

Special services were held in the above place of wor- ship on Sunday in connection with the Sunday school, and although they were the first of the kind held there, they proved a gratifying success, and greatly encouraged the superintendents and teachers. The _object of the service's was to secare funds to pay for providing the school With an entirely new set of new hymn booksand new Bibles and Testaments'. The day happily was a. .fine one, and a good congregation gathered in the morn- ing, when the. Rev. H. Dunnico preached on" Provi- dence." A number of school children occupied, a raised platform; which had been put over the com- munion, and they presented a pretty appearance. The- platform and pulpit were decorated with plants and flowers. The children and choir, to the number 'of about sixty, sang several pieces, under the leadership of Mr. J. H. Owen, of Warrington. In the afternoon the service was entirely given over to the children, and the chancel was well filled. Councillor Brough presided, and was supported on the platform by, the Revs. J. S. Hughes (pastor) and J. F. Matthews (Latchford). Miss Elsie Lyon recited the 100th Psalm, Miss Evelyn Anslow the 13th Psalm, and Miss Beatrice Holland the Ist Psalm. Ma.ster'Stanley Jones sang "Always Cheer- ful," and Master Harry Moores "Take time to be holy," while Miss Winnie Jones sang "The Shepherd's Cradle Song." Prayer was offered by the Rev. J. F. Matthews; the 'children sang 'several special hymns, and Mr. Brough gave a touching and original address on "The Prodigal Son." Mr. C.-LI. Jones, the senior superintendent, and the Rev. J. S. Hughes also spoke. As usual,•tea, was provided in the schoolroom for visitors, and over 70 persons were present, a volun- tary offering being taken to defray expenses. There Was a crowded attendance at the evening service. The preacher was the Rev. H. Minnie°. The children sang several special pieces aided by the choir. The collections were good, and the object in view will be attained. Miss Minnie Jones was the accompanist in the after- noon, and Mr. S. Brayshaw the organist at the morning and evening services. It was announced that these services would not in any way interfere with the summer sermons in June.
Warrington Company's Failure.

In the Official Receiver's Rooms, Byrom-street, Manchester, on Wednesday, a meeting was held of the creditors and contributories of the Warrington and District Electric Light and Power Company, Ltd. The statement of affairs disclosed rliabilities as be- tween the creditors and the company expected to rank £5,114 10s„ net assets £1,695 10s. 4d., and a deficiency of £3,418 135.. 6d. With £2,552 liabilities to contributories the total deficiency amounts to £5,970 13s. 6d. It was agreed that the Official Re- ceiver should apply to the court for the appointment of Messrs. Edwin Bradshaw, Watrington, and Edward Ernest Johnson, chartered accountant, of Manchester, to be liquidators, with a committee of inspection.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."

Warrington are to be congratulated on a good performance last Saturday, when they drew at Brad- ford with a score of 11 pints. The result carries out my prediction of last week, that, although Broadley's men won easily at Warrington, they would be extended pretty considerably this time. They were extended so much that it took them all their time to stave off defeat, though Warrington were short of such capable men as Isherwood, Boardman, and Morrison. A draw of eleven points each is somewhat unusual,but there is generally some free scoring when Warrington and Bradford meet. At Wilderspool on December 20th the Park Avenue men put up ten points to Warrington nil, though the homesters had a couple of tries disallowed.

Saturday's game was full of incident, and would have repaid a much larger crowd than was present. The Northern Union game, however, seems to be languishing in Bradford just now, and only about 1,500 people turned up to watch Warrington—usually a popular team. In the first five minutes Sintou put on a try for the hOmesters,but was so badly hurt after- wards that he had to retire from the game. Then Harris made a magnificent run over three parts of the field and punted past the full back only to have the misfortun:c. to be just beaten by the ball. Warrington were not long in equalising, however and the scorer was Harris who went over in dashing style, Fish kicking a goal. Warrington continued to play well and Fish added another try, the score at half time being 8 points to 3 in favour of Warrington.

Bradford quickly got -another try on res.utoino-, but it was only when Boyes, •the 'full back, placed a penalty goal that they 'drew level. Soon afterwards the WarringtOnians got a cold douche, for Fish and Hallam between them failed to . make the ball dead, and DunbaVin ran up and 'scored a "softy." The game might have been considered Bradford'snow, but Warrington rallied pluckily. Little Edmunds diddled the opposing side nicely by turning t 6 throw to Fish. The home team went for the county left winger in a body, and Edmunds neatly tossed the ball over to Dickenson, who scored easily near the posts. Fish had only to kick a goal to 4-in the match, but he failed at a very easy place. Warrington had all the play to the end, but were obliged to be content to share the pDilltS 1

On the day's play Warrington were the better team and should have won, especially after Sinton retired injured. Chances 'went begging on several occasions, and • though the backs compiled eleven points they were not at their best. Isherwoods absence, of course, made a considerable difference, but apart from this only Edmunds and Harris showed their best form. These two played grandly,in fact the wing man played the game of his life, and had the uncommon honour of a hearty reception from the crowd at the end of the game. His running was spl :ndid and he, for once, freed himself of the habit of waiting for an opponent instead of going for the line. He was easily the most dangerons man on the Warrington,side, though Fish got one try down the touch line in his own particular style. Brookes played a fair game, but I think a:trial might just as reasonably have been given to Mahoney. Hallam was poor, and but for the end of the season being onus he would probably lose his place. The forwards gave a fairly good account of themselves.

The League Ch.ampioriship is now in a very interest- ing . condition. Halifax easily beat Oldham on Saturday, and made their position more secure. They had reason to rejoice, however, when Salford went down at Hull on Monday. • The Reds were quite out- played and lost by 12 points to five, though they allege that the referee, a substitute, was incompetent. Halifax have only to make a draw of their concludinggame, at Leigh on Monday, ti? win the championsihp. The Mather-lanes are Salford's last hope, and it is quite conceivable that ,they may upset the Halifax men, especially as the latter will be none the better for playing the cup-final two days before. Salford have also another match, again at Hull, where Kingston Hovers are not likely to succumb without a struggle. The odds -for the League Championship are, now, certainly on Halifax.

Yorkshire enthusiasts seem to have buried all feeling one against the other and taken to rejoicing at the downfall of Salford. -After the match tl4 presi- dent of • the Hull Club wired to Halifax t—" We have done our best for Halifax and Yorkshire football." To this the secretary of the Halifax Club replied : "All Yorkshire, with Halifax, . appreciate your magnificent effort."
The League table up-to-date is as follows For - Agst.
Warrington nearly became the champion drawists of the League on Saturday, but their record of seven drawn games is equalled by . Swinton and. Broughton I Z a ngers.

The Northern Union Cup final will be played to- day at Leeds, where the 33,000 crowd which wit- nessed WarriVon's extinction may possibly, be ex- ceeded. The advantage of ground would seem to give Halifax the better chance, but I still have faith in Salford, who are capable of a great effort. On paper they have the better side, especially as Nettleton is announced as no playing for the Yorkshiremen. The Reds are 'putting a full team in the field, and with Lomas and his men fit they should gain .the verdict.

• A sad' fatality occurred to a well-known footballer on Wednesday night at Castle Station, Lancaster, when. John Edwin .Braithwaite, a larnpman, was knocked down by an engine during shunting opera- tions. His left leg was cut off above the knee, and his head was also injured. The unfortunate man died an hour after being admitted to the Infirmary. Braithwaite was a well-known Rugby half and three-quarter back, ~:having. played for Lancaster, Ken.dal Hornets, .St Helens,and Leeds Parish Church.

Warrington's last match takes place at home to-day, and ought to realise two points for the Wilderspool men. Huddersfield are not very formidable oppon- ents, though they • won the first engagement chiefly through the efforts of. Deere, who made Fish look rather small. The latter will have 'a chance to-day of proving that he is a better Man than the Mountain Ash international. Warrington have Selected a full team, as follows :—Hallam, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son and Harris, three-quarters; Edmunds and Duck- worth, half backs ; Boardman, Edmondson, Forster, Coleman, Naylor, Swift, Jolley, and Swift, forwards.

The Works Cotinpetition is nearing the end, the §emi-finals being down for decision on Saturday at 6.30. (Crosfield's v. ('.LC.), and on Mouthy at 6.30 (Rylands v. Naylor's or Locos). The final will be played on Wednesday, kick-off at 6.30, referee Mr. J. H. Smith, of Widnes.

The (rallies have, so far, been very well contested. There has been no kid-glove football. In fact a player in one of the recent matches, who filled a vacancy, tells me he would not play again for £5. He prefers the other side of the rails and sees more fun in shouting. This may not be the general opinion, but there is no doubt the man who is out of training feels the punishment he receives in such matches pretty -Severely.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

At the last meeting of the Committee of the War- rington Anglers' Association, a very important ques- tion was considered viz., that of re-organization. A long discuAion ensued and ultimately a scheme was evolved whereby at a somewhat reduced figure for the annual subscription, it is hoped that all anglers of the town and district may be prevailed upon to throw in their lot with the premier society, and thus by com- bination and unity of purpose, help to assist in the working, and also bearing some moiety of the expenses in the certain fishing about to be acquired. It is hoped that the more expectant anglers,will just have a little patience and then, when completed, all will be

duly published, as regards the details of proposed scheme. scheme. At the monthly meeting of the Latchford Angling Society held on Monday even- ing last, Mr. All Starkey, the Secretary announced that a substantial sum had been realised by the dance held in connection with the club. This amount has been placed to the credit of the Society. The river BoLlin is now in nice order for angling operations. Mr. R. Harrison recorded a, catch of four nice trout. last week-end, the two largest being lib Boz. 2drs. and llb respectivdly. On Monday last, Mr. Harry Green landed a large trout of 21b 6oz Bdrs. This splendid specimen has been sent to Anstiss of London to be set up. Other rods did fairly well. The excel- lent sport yielded by the Bollin just lately has given, great satisfaction amongst the members of the- Association.

Cricket. It was a melancholy coincidence that on-the day fixed for the opening of the season, representatives Of the Warrington Club should be called upon to attend the funeral of their devoted treasurer, Mr. W. IL Robinson. A most conscientious official, Mr. Robin- son, as long as health permitted, was willing to do his utmost to further the interests of the organization and by his demise a serious loss has befallen the chit It was fitting that representatives should be preseft at the interment to pay a last tribute of respect, and Mr. J. W. Bibby .(captain), Mr. C. H. Unswortli (secretary), and Mr. Thomas Cooper (secretary of the bowling club) attended. As a further mark of respect the players in the engagement • with Sefton wore a black band on the arm.

The only disappointing feature of the opening match was the extremely small attendance of specta- tors. Doubtless the weather was in some measure responsible for this. The sun shone brightly-but a cold wind made it somewhat unpleasant to watch a. cricket match.

The result of the encounter was most encouraging, and if the Warringtonians maintain their present form,the prospects for the season are decidedly bright. Sefton are old rivals of the Warrington eleven, and were strongly represented. They were the first to go to the wicket but were all dis- missed for the poor total of 38. Lynes, the Warrington professional must be accorded the greatest credit for his excellent bowling which gave the visitors so 'much :trouble.- He accounted for 7 wickets at a cost of 12 runs and in addition to bowl- ing at a fast rate he made the ball turn at such a pace that the batsmen had considerable difficulty in dealing with it. The highest score for the visitors was W, Findley, who, however, only knocked up 10 before he was caught by B. Silcock. The Warringtonians fielded. splendidly, Lynes being especially prominent in this department.

J. Callon captaineid the Warrington eleven who compiled the respectable aggregate of 79 before stumps were drawn. B. Sileock did not bat and Hampsori had scored 8 without being dismissed. The opening 'of the innings was -discouragiag, three wickets being down for eight runs. P. B. Hawtin , and W. M. Silcoek brightened the position of affairs, their combined efforts, being productive of 3g- runs. J. A. Briggs also batted in capital style, his innings realizing 13. Kitchener was the most effec- tive bowler for the visitors, capturing 8 wickets for. 37 runs. The Warrington eleven have cause to he • highly gratified at their initial success, and it is to be hoped that their good form will be itiaintained throughout the season.

The seco'n.d ele4ren visited Sefton and the engage- ment resulted in a tie, each side compiling 89. F. E. Woods was the top scorer for the visitors, being re- sponsible for 37 runs. F. Plinston knocked up 12 and D. Plinston 11. Bennett and Plinston rendered good service with the ball.

White) submitted that this was contempt of court and also a breach of defendant's oath as executor, and must be taken most strongly against him. It was a fair inter- ference to draw from the refusal to produce the account, that there were other items of a similar character to the beer engine. Mr. White further contended that there was value in the goodwill and also in the tenancy of a bowling green which the Registrar had not allowed for. The bowling green was sold at the auction sale to a representative of a brewery company for the nominal sum of one shilling, although no mention of the green was made in the advertisements of the sale. Mr. Longton said the bowling green was mentioned in the catalogue. Considerable argument ensued, Mr. White contending that the defendant had acted wrongly and improperly. in handing over the assets to Mrs. Toft instead of ad- ministering the estate and paying the creditors. Defen- dant had been purely a figurehead in the matter; _Mrs. When she having paid whatever debts that were paid. hen she found that the debts were more than she thought they were the auction sale was arranged. Mr. Longton submitted that Mr. White could have obtained any information as to the sale from the auc- tioneer. From beginning to end Mr. White had taken the case as a "fishing inquiry." lie had come before the court to obtain certain information and he had produced no evidence. His (Mr. Longton's) clients had attended on two or three occasions and pro- duced papers, documents and imforination of every imaginable kind. Mrs. Toft was sole legatee in thewill land therefore she did not take possession of anything as a stranger. Defendant told her that he would not give her any goods until all the debts were paid. An heroic attempt had been made by Mrs. Tuft and the defendant to pay the debts. The Registrar said the unpaid debts amounted to £57 7s. 11d. Mr. Longton said the defendant only found out recently that the plaintiffs' debt had not been paid. The estate had turned out to be worth less than was . anticipated and the testatrix owed more debts than defendant was aware of. Some accounts were not received until a long time after her death. In answer to the Judge,Mr. Longton said the accounts were not advertised for in the usual way. Mr. Longton, continuing, said defendant did not part with any portion of the estate. He had sold it and I divided the whole of the money among creditors, The Registrar said there were three creditors who had received nothing. Mr. Longton po;nted out that the testatrix had nothing to do with the bowling green as the late Mr. Gorse incurred all I the expenses in connection with it. His Honour said it did not seem to him that the estate had suffered any damage. Mr. Longton asked for costs for the defandant. His Honour, while complimenting Mr. White upon the able manner in which he hadconducted thecase,declined to vary the Registrar's certificate. Defendant had, however, adopted an unusual course which necessitated and justified the inquiry being held. The proper course would undoubtedly have been, to pay all debts before handing over everything to Mrs. Toft. He would, therefore, allow the plaintiffs the general costs of the action up to March 18tb. against the defendant personally. Defendant, however, was entitled to the costs of the proceedings since March 18th which .had reference to the varying of the Registrar's certificate.

THE NEW SHIPPING EXCHA...- . There has not been greater activity in any trade of recent years, especially the last half decade, than in the shipping trade : and its progress has gone forward with leaps and bounds. This week marks a distinct era in its history. On Tuesday the new Shipping Exchange opened its palatial doors in St. Mary Axe. We give a sketch of the Great Hall, which will give some idea of the magni- tude of this vast public building. It has excited general admiration and given great satisfaction, and it may well be described as the apotheosis of the Baltic. The Baltic, the great Shipping Exchange of London, which

' IVlilitary Intelligence. 11 Lieutenants E. A. Heape and R. B. Priest,of the Bury and Warrington Militia, have been awarded "special mention' at the School of Instruction at Chelsea Barracks, ',where they have been going through a course. Military Funeral. OnSunday afternoon, the remains of the late Ser- geant A. Cliffe were interred in the Warrington Cemetery with military honours. Sergeant Cliffe, who was a comparatively young man, entered the army eight years ago, joining the Ist South Lancashire Regiment. He went out to the South African war three years ago as a private, and after going through the whole of the '....ampaign, returned a few months ago a sergeant. He died on Thursday at the residence of a relative in. Factory-lane. The funeral cortege siarted from Pactory-lane, headed by a firing party, and the band of the regimental depot at Orford Barracks, and was followed by detachments of the Ist South Lancashire and King's Liverpool Regiments. The funeral service was conducted by the Rev: B- Percival, vicar of St. Peter's Church, after which the firing party fired three volleys, and the buglers gave the" Last Post." There was a very large gathering at the Cemetery to witness the last rites.
